docs.title: Verse 1.01
docs.text: PrabhandhamTirumālaiĀḻvārToṇḍaraḍippoḍi ĀḻvārArchāvatāraŚrī RaṅganāthaRasaParatattva Anubhavam

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration காவலிற் புலனை வைத்துக்கலிதனைக் கடக்கப் பாய்ந்து,நாவலிட் டுழிதரு கின்றோம்நமன்தமர் தலைகள் மீதே,மூவுல குண்டு மிழ்ந்தமுதல்வ.நின் நாமம் கற்ற,ஆவலிப் புடைமை கண்டாய்அரங்கமா நகரு ளானே. kāval il pulanai vaittukali tannai kkaḍakka ppāyndunāvaliṭṭuzi taruginṟōmnaman tamar talaigaḻ mīdēmūvulaguṇḍumizndamudalva ! nin nāmam kaṭraāvali ppuḍaimai kaṇḍāyaraṅga mā nagaruḻānē

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord! You are the primal cause who have kept and protected the three worlds within your stomach during deluge and then, made them manifest at the beginning of creation as the principal Brahman. Oh Lord residing at the great city of Srirangam! we have controlled our senses; we have indeed, leapt over the sins (and sinful deeds); and we tread on the heads of Yama and his hosts, erecting victory flagstafl's (on those heads). We are proud to say thus because of our practice of incessant chanting of your names as Sri Ranganitha, hearken!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Bhagavān holds the entire universe in His womb and hence he is called Garbhodakaśāyī Viṣṇu. As He holds the animate and inanimate within His garbha, He is also called Hiraṇyagarbha. From this Hiraṇyagarbha, everything is created. In the Pāñcarātra Āgama, the expansion of Vāsudeva, i.e., Saṅkarṣaṇa, further expands as Garbhodakaśāyī Viṣṇu, holding the entire universe within Him. Āḻvār praises the Lord for protecting us all the time, even after pralaya. Once He decides to create the universe again, with His saṅkalpa alone, He creates the lotus-born Brahmā. Due to Him being the primal cause of everything, He is the Brahman. This Supreme Brahman resides in Śrīraṅgam on the bed of Ādiśeṣa.

Our senses (Indriyas) play a primary role in performing actions. The mind among them can either distract us from the primary goal (Brahman) or attract us towards Him. Once one controls his senses, he is able to leap over all sinful activities. All the results of the pious actions the jīvatma performs are surrendered at the lotus feet of the Lord. When one becomes a Prapanna, surrendering to the divine feet of the Lord, he is able to conquer the cycle of birth and death (personified by Ālvār as treading on the head of Yama). One can only attain liberation by chanting the beautiful names of the Lord. By chanting the Thirumantram, that yogi is able to enter the Supreme above where the Nityas sing the glories of the Supreme.

docs.title: Verse 1.02

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration பச்சைமா மலைபோல் மேனிபவளவாய் கமலச் செங்கண்அச்சுதா. அமர ரேறே.ஆயர்தம் கொழுந்தே. என்னும்,இச்சுவை தவிர யான்போய்இந்திர லோக மாளும்,அச்சுவை பெறினும் வேண்டேன்அரங்கமா நகரு ளானே paccai mā malai pōl mēnipavaḻa vāy kamala cceṅgaṇaccudā ! amarar ēṟē !āyar tam kozundē ! ennumiccuvai tavira yān pōyindira lōgam āḻumaccuvai peṟinum vēṇḍēnaraṅga mā nagaruḻānē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord Acyuta possessing a huge, emarald mountain like body, rosy lip of precious corals, and reddish lotus-like eyes! "Oh Lord of the Nityasuris of the Paramapadham! O dear young lad of the cowherds!" thus do I like to chant forever. If so I don't have the chance to chant your holy name at Vaikunta, let that mokasha be never given. How will I ever leave the elixir taste of chanting "Ranga!" at Srirangam and go there? Oh Lord of Thiruvarangam!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: Toṇḍaraḍippoḍi Āḻvār sings the glories of the beautiful thirumeni of Bhagavān. He narrates by personifying the thirumukham of Bhagavān. His lips are smooth like pearls and corals. The color of his lips resembles that of a rose. His eyes, which can attract any jīvatma (and hence are red by their nature of attraction), look like lotus petals. His thirumeni is as huge as mountains and shines like emeralds. He is the Lord of Nityasuris, who rules Paramapadham. If the Lord decides to grant Ālvār the capacity to rule Vaikuṇṭham itself, but if there he could not sing about Ranga, Ālvār says, "What is the use of such liberation if I cannot enjoy Your glorious names? After tasting the elixir called Nāma Saṅkīrtanam here in Śrīraṅgam, I deny such liberation! Oh Lord of Śrīraṅgam!"

docs.title: Verse 1.03

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration வேதநூல் பிராயம் நூறுமனிசர்தாம் புகுவ ரேலும்,பாதியு முறங்கிப் போகும்நின்றதில் பதினை யாண்டு,பேதைபா லகன தாகும்பிணிபசி மூப்புத் துன்பம்,ஆதலால் பிறவி வேண்டேன்அரங்கமா நகரு ளானே. vēda nūl pirāyam nūṟumaniśar tām puguvarēlumpādiyum uṟaṅgi ppōgumninṟadil padinai āṇḍupēdai pālagan adāgumpiṇi paśi mūppu ttunbamādalāl piṟavi vēṇḍēnaraṅga mā nagaruḻānē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord who recides in Srirangam, the Vedas and Shastras are many and are huge. Life span of lofty humans like us doesn't cross 100. In those years, we spend half of it by sleeping. The other half is spent in childhood, youth, old age filled with misery. Oh Ranga! In this run of life this birth leaches out most of the time leaving very little to perform Kainkaryam to you. Hence, I ask you Lord of Thiruvarangam, I do not want to be born again.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Vedas and Śāstras prescribe multiple ways known as Brahma Vidyā, which often require the jīvatma to perform upāsana. But these Śāstras are vast in number, with thousands of texts. The human lifespan itself falls short of 100 years (and gets shorter). How is it possible to explore the Vedas with such limited time in which we spend most of it sleeping and the other half indulging in temporary pleasure and pain? What is the use of such a birth where one cannot perform service to the divine Lord? No doubt, after spending such a life, the jīvatma is reborn in this saṃsāra.

Hence, Ālvār pleads to Ranganātha not to grant him rebirth. If such a birth denies performing service to the Lord, what is the use of it? Therefore, Ālvār requests Ranganātha to grant Paramapadham. (In the previous pāsuram, Ālvār stated that if in such Paramapadham there is no bliss of chanting the names of the Lord, he denies it. But in reality, the Taittirīya Upaniṣad states that the Nityas and Mukhtas keep singing the glories of the Lord. Hence, in this pāsuram, Ālvār requests to grant such a liberation.)

docs.title: Verse 1.04

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration மொய்த்தவல் வினையுள் நின்றுமூன்றெழுத் துடைய பேரால்,கத்திர பந்து மன்றேபராங்கதி கண்டு கொண்டான்,இத்தனை யடிய ரானார்க்கிரங்கும்நம் மரங்க னாயபித்தனைப் பெற்று மந்தோ.பிறவியுள் பிணங்கு மாறே moytta val vinaiyuḻ ninṟumūnṟezuttuḍaiya pērālkattira pandum anṟēparāṅgadi kaṇḍu koṇḍānittanai aḍiyar ānārkkuiraṅgum nam araṅganāyapittanai ppeṭrum andō !piṟaviyuḻ piṇaṅgumāṟē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Kṣtrabandhu, son of Viśvavrata, performed such vikarmas which resulted in him accumulating tremendous sins. Just by uttering the name "Govinda," he was released from all sins. Alas! You are here as the supreme Master Raṅganātha, who showers His grace just by looking at the devotee. I am indeed surprised that when You are here to grant the abode itself to the devoted chanters, why are people still ignorant and indulged in saṃsāric activities?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Govinda nāma is considered very auspicious and precious due to the beautiful meaning behind it. Govinda refers to the protector of Earth (a reference to the Varāha avatāra). It also refers to Him being the protector of cows as Gopāla. It infers that He is the protector of the ones who surrender to Him. Hence He is also praised as prapanna pārijāta. Āḻvār specifically refers to this name here relating to the goal of liberation from the cycle of saṃsāra. Once one surrenders to the lotus feet of His, that jīvātmā has Vaikuṇṭha assured to him. The Lord in the form of Varāha promised it as "ahaṃ smarāmi madbhaktaṃ nayāmi paramāṃ gatim," i.e., "Those who remember me when they are healthy, I will grant them the supreme abode." Again as Kṛṣṇa, He stated "mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja ahaṁ tvāṁ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ," i.e., "Abandon all other means to attain mokṣa, just surrender to me. I myself will be the means and take care of removing all your sins and grant salvation to you. Do not fear!" Hence, the nāma Govinda infers these meanings of the specific avatāras. The protector of Bhū Devī, the protector of cows, will indeed protect us from this saṃsāra!

Āḻvār is surprised now! Even after the Supreme established such an easy means to attain Him, just by chanting His divinity, alas! Why are people still bound by māyā, running after temporary materialistic things?

docs.title: Verse 1.05

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration பெண்டிரால் சுகங்க ளுய்ப்பான்பெரியதோ ரிடும்பை பூண்டுஉண்டிராக் கிடக்கும் போதுஉடலுக்கே கரைந்து நைந்து,தண்டுழாய் மாலை மார்பன்தமர்களாய்ப் பாடி யாடி,தொண்டுபூண் டமுத முண்ணாத்தொழும்பர்சோ றுகக்கு மாறே peṇḍirāl śugaṅgaḻ uyppānperiyadōr iḍumbai pūṇḍuuṇḍirā kkiḍakkum pōduuḍalukkē karaindu naindutaṇ tuzāy mālai mārbantamargaḻāy ppāḍi āḍitoṇḍu pūṇḍamudam uṇṇātozumbar śōṟugakkumāṟē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Men of vile nature alone seek the pleasure of enjoying women; they suffer from untold miseries; they serve others to eke out their livelihood; they don't find time to eat properly, (and so) eat only late at night; and then, they only lie down and brood over their pitiable body alone. If at all, men could distinguish their self from body, they can surrender to the Lord Raṅganātha whose chest is adorned with the garland of cool tulasī leaves and become His devotees. Then they can enjoy singing His names and dancing in ecstasy — thus by doing such a divine service, they can taste the nectarine bliss. But, alas! The vile persons are mad after (mundane) food alone, and not the divine nectar.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār continues to condemn the nature of saṃsāric men, devoid of understanding of the divine nectar of nāma saṅkīrtana due to their temporary happiness obtained in their world of ignorance. These men are after saṃsāric pleasures which are obtained by pleasuring the indriyas. Indulged in trying to obtain such pleasures, they forget to maintain their body which is granted to perform kaiṅkaryam to Bhagavān. The ignorance which gives birth to such men is from the fact that they are unable to realize that they (the jīvātmā) are different from the body.

Due to this, they try to please the body alone, giving it the utmost importance. When they lack the knowledge of difference between jīvātmā and śarīra, how can they even know Raṅganātha who is the Self of the jīvātmā itself as Antaryāmī? How can they enjoy the nectar which is obtained by serving that Raṅganātha who always wears a tulasī garland? Devoid of such beautiful spiritual love, the vile persons run behind food and women. They sow the seeds of rebirth, disabling the chances of salvation.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration மறம்சுவர் மதிளெ டுத்துமறுமைக்கே வெறுமை பூண்டு,புறம்சுவ ரோட்டை மாடம்புரளும்போ தறிய மாட்டீர்,அறம்சுவ ராகி நின்றஅரங்கனார்க் காட்செய் யாதே,புறம்சுவர் கோலஞ் செய்துபுள்கவ்வக் கிடக்கின் றீரே maṟam śuvar madiḻ eḍuttumaṟumaikkē veṟumai pūṇḍupuṟam śuvar ōṭṭai māḍampuraḻum pōdaṟiya māṭṭīraṟam śuvar āgi ninṟaaraṅganārkkāṭ ceyyādēpuṟam śuvar kkōlañjeydupuḻ kauva kkiḍakkinṟīrē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: O idiotic men! You do not know when you are to die, for you are building the fort of adharma (māyā) and you ever think of your perishable body as a cover (of protection); you are increasing your poverty by sowing the seeds of rebirth. It is a pity that you don't take to the divine service under the great Lord of Śrīraṅgam, the supreme Wall of Dharma. Therefore, you are just engrossed in nourishing (and taking care of) your outer wall of śarīra which the vultures would eventually tear into pieces.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: Continuing from the previous pāsuram, Āḻvār continues to question the deeds of the idiotic men who are behind saṃsāric pleasures. Unable to realize the perishable character of this body, their mind is covered by māyā. They keep performing actions which pleasure the indriyas. While doing so, they forget to realize they can be adharmic. Addicted to that temporary pleasure, they keep performing the same actions again and again, leading them to create a huge pitfall of adharma itself! They might be rich materialistically, but alas! They are poor in reality as rebirth is assured to such fools. Eventually, he loses everything, even his body perishes. What is the use of nourishing that body with all care and no efforts taken to use that body to serve the Īśvara, the Lord of Śrīraṅgam who is the protector of Dharma himself! Such fools perish stuck in the cycle of saṃsāra!

docs.title: Verse 1.07

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration புலையற மாகி நின்றபுத்தொடு சமண மெல்லாம்,கலையறக் கற்ற மாந்தர்காண்பரோ கேட்ப ரோதாம்,தலையறுப் புண்டும் சாவேன்சத்தியங் காண்மின் ஐயா,சிலையினா லிலங்கை செற்றதேவனே தேவ னாவான் pulai aṟam āgi ninṟaputtoḍu śamaṇam ellāmkalai aṟakkaṭra māndarkāṇbarō kēṭparō tāmtalai aṟuppuṇḍum śāvēnśattiyam kāṇmin aiyāśilaiyināl ilaṅgai śeṭratēvanē tēvan āvān

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: This is the noble truth! Those who are well-versed in Vedānta and Śāstras are not misled by the teachings of Jaina and Buddhist doctrines. Without a doubt, they realize that Rāma alone is the Brahman! I claim hereby that I will shave my head from my body and am ready to die if what I have stated is wrong, i.e., the vanquisher of ten-headed Rāvaṇa and the holder of Śārṅga is the Supreme Lord.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḷvār boldly claims without a doubt that Śrī Rāmacandra is Brahman! He is the Supreme Lord. With the rise of different philosophies and theologies, it is possible for our monkey-like brains to be deluded by various confusing statements. The Śākyas (i.e., Buddhists) and the Jainas deny the existence of a Supreme personality who is the Īśvara, the controller of all. On the other hand, Tāntric texts mislead by stating other devatās are the Supreme Brahman. But unlike these philosophies or texts, Vedas are apauruṣeya, i.e., there is no date which can be stated when the Vedas were created. They were not created by any human. For ages, they have been passed to the next generation through communication between Ācārya and Śiṣya. Even when the universe undergoes dissolution, they are always protected by the Brahman.

That Veda, which shines due to its speaking about the Brahman, states that Nārāyaṇa is that Supreme Lord who has none second to him. The Nārāyaṇopaniṣad of Taittirīya states this explicitly as nirākhyātaḥ śuddho deva eko nārāyaṇaḥ । na dvitīyo'sti kaścit । When the eternal Vedas themselves state without a doubt that Nārāyaṇa (Śrī Rāma) is the Paratattvam, Āḷvār states there is no doubt that the one who slayed the ruler of Laṅkā and holds the bow called Śārṅga is indeed the one who will liberate us from this cycle of Saṃsāra. It has to be noted that Āḷvār condemns the actions of those followers of other faiths who don't show respect towards Bhagavān. As per Āḷvārs, they are least concerned about condemning people unless it comes to the fact that those people speak ill of Bhagavān.

docs.title: Script

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord of the great city, Śrīraṅgam! If at all the bitter Jains and Śaivites and the unlucky Buddhists (Śākyas) are to deliver unendurable tenets of adharma and to insult you, O Lord, they will certainly perish and their faiths will not last long, because their speech itself becomes the incurable illness. And this is my wish: I would surely chop off their heads, if I am able and eligible, for they do not censure me alone, but even insult the supreme Godhead, Lord Raṅganātha.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: Continuing from the previous pāsuram, Āḷvār expresses his anger towards those who speak ill of the Lord. For Āḷvārs, Raṅganātha was their dear child, their husband, their everything. In this pāsuram, Āḷvār speaks as sharp as a sword to those who speak ill of the Lord. Just as it is not possible for a mother to hear her child being spoken ill of by someone, Āḷvār cannot tolerate when others deny the Parattva of Nārāyaṇa. Āḷvār calls them unlucky and unfortunate. They are indeed following adharma by insulting Bhagavān. When the Vedas themselves are focused towards that Raṅganātha, insulting him is adharmic without a doubt. These will certainly perish as their speech itself becomes a disease to those fools! Unable to tolerate such words, Āḷvār is ready to slay them if he had the chance to do so, i.e., if Āḷvār were eligible to do so. But doing that would be asāttvic and would not bring glory to our Lord. It's clear from this pāsuram that Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḷvār (and other Āḷvārs as well) cannot tolerate anyone who insults Raṅganātha, the Nātha of the entire universe.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh people incapable of reasoning! Is there any God other than Śrīman Nārāyaṇa? None at all. You cannot know Him (Śriyaḥ-pati), because you do not recognize Him as the supreme Master, owing to your immature logic. Whatever is the most Supreme, i.e., beyond your ken, you are not ready to understand. Know Him, Lord Nārāyaṇa alone as God. There is no God other than Him. May you resort to Him (Lord Raṅganātha), nay, to His unexcelled pair of feet, the Lord who, as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, tended the hosts of grazing cows.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: Āḷvār continues to speak to us that without a doubt the one who has Śrī as his divine consort, the one who houses her on his chest is the Supreme Lord indeed! In the previous pāsuram, Āḷvār proves the Parattva of the Lord in his Śrī Rāma avatāra; here he does the same with Śrī Kṛṣṇa as Gopāla. He calls those who cannot understand the fact that Śrīman Nārāyaṇa is supreme as people who cannot reason; their minds have rotted and hence are unable to think critically and logically. Indeed these people are fools! These immature-minded fools think that the cowherd Kṛṣṇa is a mere human. To such personalities, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself quotes in Bhagavad Gītā: "avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā mānuṣīṁ tanum āśritam," i.e., "Fools deride Me when I descend in the human form." Āḷvār questions those: what can make you fools understand that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Lord? Indeed there is no one second to him. He alone is the Īśvara and not any other devatā. To those who have realized it, surrender to his lotus feet! Surrender to him who tends and protects the grazing cows (again Āḷvār refers to Bhagavān as Govinda, the protector of cows as well as Śaraṇāgatas).

docs.text: Tamil Transliteration நாட்டினான் தெய்வ மெங்கும்நல்லதோ ரருள்தன் னாலே,காட்டினான் திருவ ரங்கம்உய்பவர்க் குய்யும் வண்ணம்,கேட்டிரே நம்பி மீர்காள்.கெருடவா கனனும் நிற்க,சேட்டைதன் மடிய கத்துச்செல்வம்பார்த் திருக்கின் றீரே nāṭṭinān teyvam eṅgumnalladōr aruḻ tannālēkāṭṭinān tiruvaraṅgamuybavarkkuyyum vaṇṇamkēṭṭirē nambimīrgāḻ !keruḍa vāgananum niṟkaśēṭṭai tan maḍiyagattuśelvam pārttirukkinṟīrē

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Just as the primordial Deity (Śrīman Nārāyaṇa) established many gods throughout the world, even so He has revealed Himself as Śrī Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam for the sake of the aspirants, out of His unbounded compassion. I beseech you, O believers of the Vedas and Śāstras! Listen to me. While there is our Lord with the supreme divine Garuḍa as His vehicle, why do you expect prosperity at the lap of Jyeṣṭhā?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Īśvara, Śrīman Nārāyaṇa has revealed himself to humans as Raṅganātha due to his Dayā. To nityas and muktas he appears as Para Vāsudeva and to ṛṣis as Antaryāmī. To devatās he blessed them in Vyūha, but to mere humans like us these forms are inaccessible. To pave a path for us towards Arcāvatāra mārga, to quench our thirst to serve him, he has appeared in Thiruvaraṅgam as Śrī Raṅganātha, ready to accept our service. For the Supreme being himself to appear in the form of Arcā and accept all the service we provide to him, Āḷvār exclaims, how great is his compassion! Indeed it has no bounds just like the ocean!

Next, Āḷvār explains how Garuḍa is the personification of Veda itself. Garuḍa is known to be the vehicle of Bhagavān. Garuḍa is Vedas personified. The Vedas glorify Śrīman Nārāyaṇa. Just as it holds and carries the glories of the Lord, so does Garuḍa. The two wings are said to represent the two divisions of the Sāma Veda, known as bṛhat and rathantara. Garuḍa's eyes are said to be the Gāyatrī mantra, which protects those who chant it. Just as the mantras travel from one world to another at the speed of light, so does Garuḍa. Āḷvār states to us, think about the Lord who rides the personification of Vedas itself. When he is ready to welcome us like a father to his children, why are we still unable to understand his compassion and end up stuck in this Saṃsāra, which is the greatest misfortune!

docs.text: Tamil Transliteration ஒருவில்லா லோங்கு முந்நீர்அனைத்துல கங்க ளுய்ய,செருவிலே யரக்கர் கோனைச்செற்றநம் சேவ கனார்,மருவிய பெரிய கோயில்மதிள்திரு வரங்க மென்னா,கருவிலே திருவி லாதீர்.காலத்தைக் கழிக்கின் றீரே oru villāl ōṅgu munnīr aḍaittuulagaṅgaḻ uyyaśeruvilē arakkar kōnaiśeṭra nam śēvaganārmaruviya periya kōyilmadil tiruvaraṅgam ennākaruvilē tiru ilādīr !kālattai kkazikkinṟīrē

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Periya Kōyil (the great Temple) is the shrine (of Lord Śrī Raṅganātha) with seven massive ramparts (prākāras). One should ever think of Śrīraṅgam, the abode of Raṅganātha, where our supreme Lord has permanently reclined on the Serpent-couch (Ādiśeṣa). Śrī Raṅganātha is our mighty Lord who, in his advent as Śrī Rāma, has slain Rāvaṇa, the demon-king, in battle, after constructing the bridge (setu) across the roaring ocean, for the sake of retrieving all the worlds by his inimitable Bow (Śārṅga). Oh men without the grace of the Lord (Raṅganātha) even when you were in the mother's womb! Why do you waste your time without chanting the name of Śrīraṅgam? Alas!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: Āḷvār continues to glorify the greatness of chanting the divine names of Bhagavān. Here, he emphasises us to remember Śrīraṅgam, the divine abode of Śrī Raṅganātha. The great temple is surrounded by seven prākāras which cover overall a tremendous area of 157 acres. Like a treasure protected by several outer coating chests, the Supreme Lord, who is the ultimate goal of life, the true treasure is lying on Ādiśeṣa at the center of these prākāras. Āḷvār speaks to us to remember that Śrīraṅgam which hosts the divine Lord. Raṅganātha, who is non-different from Śrī Rāmacandra, destroyed the king of Laṅkā with his inimitable bow, the Śārṅga. Āḷvār questions us, calling us foolish to not remember him. The whole universe remains stable due to his Saṅkalpa Śakti alone just like the pearls are withheld by a thread ("mayi sarvaṃ idaṃ protaṃ sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva"). Without his Saṅkalpa Śakti, neither would the universe be created or sustained nor would any of us be born from the womb of our mothers. He is the controller of all and hence is the Īśvara, and our not remembering him is the most unfortunate thing and it is the greatest waste of time, Āḷvār states.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration நமனும்முற் கலனும் பேசநரகில்நின் றார்கள் கேட்க,நரகமே சுவர்க்க மாகும்நாமங்க ளுடைய நம்பி,அவனதூ ரரங்க மென்னாதுஅயர்த்துவீழ்ந் தளிய மாந்தர்,கவலையுள் படுகின் றாரென்றதனுக்கே கவல்கின் றேனே namanum muṟkalanum pēśanaragil ninṟārgaḻ kēṭkanaragamē śuvarkkam āgumnāmaṅgaḻ uḍaiya nambiavanadūr araṅgam ennāduayarttu vīzndaḻiya māndarkavalaiyuḻ paḍuginṟār enṟuadanukkē kavalginṟēnē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Raṅganātha, whose name you can ever chant and be rid of miseries! Oh supreme Lord with all the auspicious qualities and endowed with numerous divine names! When Yama and sage Mudgala were conversing with each other (i.e., when Mudgala referred to Your divine names), and when those residing in the hell (the abode of Yama) heard Your divine names, the hell was, indeed, fortunate to turn itself into heaven (because of the greatness of Your names). When there are so many divine names of Yours, I am very much worried about the people who fall down out of miseries and are afflicted by sorrow. Because of ignorance, they do not know Your divine grace and the efficacy of your divine names and the divine abode Śrīraṅgam.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The remembrance of Bhagavān can remove any sins and grant divine liberation itself. It can indeed even convert the depths of hell into the great heavens itself. Āḷvār proves this point by remembering the incident which took place in hell when Mudgala was taken there. When Yama and Ṛṣi Mudgala are having a conversation about the dynamics which the jīvātmā suffers when it is subjected in hell and the pleasure in heaven, the great seer speaks about how these are temporary and chants the name of Nārāyaṇa which would grant Paramapada itself. On chanting the nāma of Nārāyaṇa once, hell for a second turned into heaven. The jīvātmās who with a Sūkṣma Śarīra were subjected to pain according to their Karmas, were liberated from such torture and pious birth was given to them. Such are the glories of chanting the divine names of Bhagavān which would burn Karmas of those who even listen to it.

How great are the glories of the Lord's names, which can burn the sins of the greatest sinners. Our Lord possesses infinite divine qualities and hence infinite divine names. Āḷvār is astonished by the fact that even after having such an easy route to burn down our Karma, i.e., by chanting his divine names, even after knowing that he possesses not just one or two but countless such names, how foolish are people who are engaged in Saṃsāric activities forgetting about the Divine. Due to their ignorance and arrogance, they are destined to fall and be stuck in this cycle of saṃsāra. How unfortunate are these who do not realize the glories of Your divine grace and Your divine abode, Śrīraṅgam.

docs.text: Tamil Transliteration எறியுநீர் வெறிகொள் வேலைமாநிலத் துயிர்க ளெல்லாம்,வெறிகொள்பூந் துளவ மாலைவிண்ணவர் கோனை யேத்த,அறிவிலா மனித ரெல்லாம்அரங்கமென் றழைப்ப ராகில்,பொறியில்வாழ் நரக மெல்லாம்புல்லெழுந் தொழியு மன்றே? eṟiyu nīr veṟi koḻ vēlaimā nilattuyirgaḻ ellāmveṟi koḻ pūn tuḻava mālaiviṇṇavar kōnai ēttaaṟivilā maniśar ellāmaraṅgam enṟazaippar āgilpoṟiyil vāz naragam ellāmpul ezundoziyum anṟē

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Men of high calibre — viz., those who reside in many dvīpas and many varṣas, surrounded by the tidal oceans and scented sea-shores — extol the supreme (Lord of Nityasūris) adorned with the garland of Tulasī with great fragrance. But those who lack the knowledge to praise the supreme Lord, even if they could just utter the name of the holy city Śrīraṅgam as 'Araṅgam', it is enough (for them to destroy their sins). Thus when all people get freed from sins, there won't be anyone to go to hell; and so, the hell will be bereft of any souls (to suffer for their sins), and thus there would be only grass growing; and later on, the hell itself would become extinct. Isn't it?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: Āḷvār states that the seers and ṛṣis are able to praise the Lord who always wears the tulasī garland. Indeed, these are the Nityasūris who are serving the Lord eternally, singing his glories. The Viṣṇu Sūktam states the same as "tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ." The supreme Lord blesses knowledge to the Ṛṣis and hence they are able to sing his glories. To people like us who lack such knowledge, chanting the divine residence of Raṅganātha, i.e., "Araṅgam" itself would destroy all the Karma which acts as the blocker for us to reach the divine. Āḷvār states, if every jīvātmā stuck here in this Saṃsāra (he calls this Bhūloka as Naraka as we are bounded by Indriyas and suffering due to it) uttered the great names of Bhagavān, then this saṃsāra would be devoid of any jīvātmā as all of them would have attained liberation, making this place a wasteland. Though this is certainly hypothetical as there are countless jīvātmās, yet Āḷvār tries to exclaim that such is the glory of the names of the Supreme that it can liberate any jīvātmā.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: In Śrīraṅgam, there are the resounding gardens full of innumerable humming honey-bees; there are also many gardens beautified by many flocks of dancing peacocks; there are also many bowers which rise up to the height of clouds (Kōṇḍal). Especially, Śrīraṅgam is the holy temple-town where the God of gods eternally resides. And so, Śrīraṅgam is extremely beautiful and lovable. Those who do not recite the name of Thiru Araṅgam are, indeed, arrogant people of haughtiness/foolishness. Therefore, Oh people! Remove forcibly the food which they (the ignorant and arrogant men) eat greedily, from their mouth, and serve it to dogs which are better than those arrogant men.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: Āḻvār explains how beautiful Śrīraṅgam is. Śrīraṅgam is situated near the river banks of Kāvērī and its tributary Kollidam. Due to the rich river basin present, the island-like city has beautiful nature and plants. Because of this, several honey bees roam around the place. Peacocks are another unique bird which are always present in Śrīraṅgam. It is not surprising that Śrīraṅgam has such beautiful nature. This is due to the fact that the Īśvara of the universe resides as Raṅganātha, lying on the bed of Ādiśeṣa. Indeed, there cannot be such a place which is so lovable. Those people who refuse to recite the divine name of Thirurangam are arrogant. They are living in ignorance. Āḻvār quotes a statement which can be seen in Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa in the conversation between Śiva and Nārada. Śiva states to Nārada that those who refuse to chant the divine name of Raṅganātha, deny giving food to them. It's better to give that food to the dogs who reside in Śrīraṅgam rather than giving it to such a cheap personality.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: The Lord Viṣṇu who has Garuḍa on His banner, is eternally real for those who acknowledge Him as real. But He is unreal to those who themselves are unreal, because of their atheistic attitude like me who am untruthful. The Lord Viṣṇu, viz. the Lord of the beautiful city Śrīraṅgam, reveals Himself to those who aspire for Ujjīvanam, cuts asunder all their doubts and grants the supreme knowledge that He is the only one supreme Person. Isn't it?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār expresses the graceful nature of the Lord who grants divine knowledge to people who show unadulterated devotion towards him. When Gajendra offered him a lotus by calling him "Ādimūla," without a second's delay he appeared in front of the elephant to rescue him. Hence, he always listens to the calls of his pure devotees. Even to those who lack complete knowledge, he grants it to them slowly. He is compassionate to all his devotees, irrespective of the level of knowledge they have. Ultimately, he takes the responsibility that they attain him eventually.

On the other hand are the foolish atheists who deny his existence. They will never be able to see his divine form. Because of their Tāmasic Guṇa, they see him as non-existent, which has occurred due to ignorance. Hence to those untruthful fools, he remains hidden. Āḻvār, practicing nikṛṣṭa bhakti, expresses himself as the lowest among personalities and tries to express his gratitude to the Lord for showing divine grace on him.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: I was once a gambler and a thief, ensnared in the love-nets of fish-eyed women. But the beautiful Lord commanded, "Come forth!" He entered my mind and kindled my love for Him. Indeed, Raṅganātha permeated my being and ignited my devotion. Is it not so that He protected a helpless soul like me from the clutches of saṃsāra?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār narrates how the Lord transformed his life, redirecting his love from materialistic pleasures to Raṅganātha. Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḻvār was once mesmerized by the beauty of a dancer named Dēvadēvi. Her eyes, resembling fish, were captivating. Consequently, his interest, initially focused on Raṅganātha, gradually shifted towards Dēvi. However, the Lord always safeguards those who surrender to Him. When their minds stray from the spiritual path, He assumes the responsibility of guiding them back. Āḻvār's poverty was humiliated by Dēvadēvi's mother. Raṅganātha Himself brought a golden vessel to Dēvadēvi's house, introducing Himself as Āḻvār's disciple.

Alas! The golden vessel was no ordinary object, but one used for nitya kaiṅkaryam in Śrīraṅgam to serve the Lord. When the temple discovered the vessel's loss and its presence in Dēvi's house, the king intervened and arrested Āḻvār. Āḻvār soon realized how misguided he had been from his true path of life and lamented his sinful ways. Raṅganātha promptly appeared to the king and ordered Āḻvār's release, declaring him very dear to Him. The Lord of Thiruvaraṅgam enacted such beautiful līlās with the Āḻvārs, demonstrating His personal care for the prapannas. For the śaraṇāgatas, He Himself ensures they remain on the right path, assuring liberation from saṃsāra. Indeed, He enters into these prapannas and inspires them to show Him the utmost possible love.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: I know neither how to praise You nor how to love You adequately, O Lord! Neither am I able to glorify You with my tongue nor follow the scriptures righteously. Yet, how compassionate You are! O Lord of Śrīraṅgam, whose land is always filled with the melodious buzzing of bees, You entered my heart like molten iron, slowly melting it, enabling me to witness Your divine Thirumēṉi. How fortunate are my eyes, which are delighted to behold Your ever-radiant form!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār expresses how fortunate his eyes are to witness the divine form of Raṅganātha. He narrates that he knows not how to praise the Lord, as His guṇas are infinite in nature. When Prajāpati Brahmā himself cannot fully glorify the Lord's form, how can we mere mortals hope to do so? We are unable to show the unadulterated love towards the Lord like the gopīs. When it comes to following the scriptures, which are the divine words of Bhagavān, we are most inaccurate.

We fail to perform the prescribed activities, instead engaging in vikarmas that should be avoided. Yet, how compassionate is the Supreme Lord! Āḻvār expresses the saulabhya guṇa of Bhagavān. That Para Vāsudeva, who is the Īśvara of the universe, reclines here on Ādiśeṣa in the form of arcā, ready to accept any service offered to Him. He entered Āḻvār's heart like molten iron, slowly melting it. This ignited divine love in Āḻvār's heart towards Bhagavān, enabling him to witness the Lord's divine form. Āḻvār emphasizes that Bhagavān Himself is the reason for such divine love.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord, who reclines on Ādiśeṣa in Śrīraṅgam, I am unable to withstand the beauty of Your divine form. Those rosy lips resembling bimba fruits and the red lotus-like eyes are mesmerizing my mind. You have reclined on the divine ocean whose waters are cool and soothing. What a sinner am I that my tears obstruct the view of Your divine form!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Continuing from the previous pāsuram, Āḻvār narrates the exquisite beauty of Bhagavān's divine form. Similar to the second pāsuram of Tirumalai, Āḻvār expresses his unbearable love for Bhagavān's divine form. That divya maṅgala rūpa possesses soft, rosy lips and eyes resembling lotus petals (kamala-nayana). Indeed, His form is mesmerizing, and whoever beholds it is stunned. Our minds can scarcely imagine a spark of such glory.

Witnessing such a divine form, it is impossible for the devoted Āḻvār to hold back his tears. As they flow from his eyes, they hinder Āḻvār's view of the divine Lord. Āḻvār laments what a sinner he must be, unable to fully enjoy the Lord's divine form! Bhagavān's divya maṅgala rūpa, once seen, makes any devotee yearn to gaze upon it again and again. Unable to view His divine form is separation from Him, and thus Āḻvār cries out that his tears obstruct his view.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: You have placed Your crowned head towards the West, and towards the East, You have stretched Your legs, revealing those beautiful lotus feet. To the Northern direction, You have shown Your back, and You sleep on Ādiśeṣa facing South where Laṅkā stands. Oh my! After beholding the Supreme Lord as Śrīraṅganātha, my body melts! What can I do?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: The divine Lord of Śrīraṅgam, Raṅganātha, reclines on the bed of Ādiśeṣa, but what is His posture? Āḻvār narrates this to us. His divine crown rests towards the West, and His lotus feet rest towards the East. To the North, He shows His back, while He faces Laṅkā by looking South. Fulfilling His promise to Vibhīṣaṇa to always watch over his kingdom, Raṅganātha faces towards Laṅkā. The Lord's crown echoes, "The Lord here is the Supreme Brahman." When a devotee beholds the crown, they might fear that Īśvara Himself is present, but the Lord's smile assures that although He is Īśvara, He is also Bhaktavatsala. He indeed yearns to meet us and shower grace upon us. While His right hand gestures towards the crown, indicating His status as Īśvara, His left hand points to His lotus feet. The Lord speaks to us, inviting us to surrender to Him and assuring us that He will take care of our material and spiritual progress. After witnessing such a divine form, how can one remain still? Āḻvār, whose devotion surpasses ours, is unable to maintain composure. His body trembles in ecstasy upon beholding the Thirumēṉi of Raṅganātha.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: How can a devotee refrain from reveling in Your divine form? The magnificent form of Yours in Śrīraṅgam, reclining on the bed called Ādiśeṣa. That broad chest of Yours where Śrī Herself resides. Your Thirumēṉi, beautiful to behold like majestic mountains, with its emerald hue. How can a devotee resist, even after glimpsing those rosy lips, coral mouth, and the ever-captivating lotus-like eyes!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār, in response to saṃsārins questioning why he suffers in bhagavad viṣayam, causing his body to melt and eyes to shed tears, instead of joining them in enjoying the pleasures of saṃsāra, describes the beauty of the Lord. He states that this beauty is for bhaktas to enjoy, asking rhetorically, "How can one go away from that?" He notes that holier things take shelter at Śrīraṅgam. He observes that the environment of Śrīraṅgam is conducive for them not to be polluted by saṃsāra. He describes how the river Kāveri happily flows around Śrī Raṅganāthan. Āḻvār points out that over the water, the Lord has spread His Ādiśeṣan bed. He states that the Lord is engaged in yōganidrā. While seen in standing and sitting postures in many divyadeśams, here He is seen as an elephant resting on the ground. The Āḻvār suggests that seeing Him in such a beautiful posture transcends one somewhere, and that perhaps this beauty alone brings us towards Him, which is magical.

Āḻvār notes that with the presence of Mahālakṣmī, the Lord's broad chest has become a special part of His divine body. He compares the Lord's appearance to a flood of water, a cool sight for the eyes. He likens the Lord's shoulders to a float for bhaktas to grab and come up when they sink in the enjoyment of seeing other divine limbs. He describes the cool kaṭākṣam (divine glance) of the Lord's eyes, which does not change whether He sees Mahālakṣmī or Hiraṇyakaśipu. Āḻvār states that such a cool glance should not be compared even with the finest earthly things like cool gentle breeze and lotus flower, as these are good for some and terrible for others. Hence, he prefixes the adjective 'tūya' (pristine pure) to His glance. He notes that the divine mouth with reddish lips and rows of teeth attracts all sorts of people, whether they are jñānis or pāpis. He indicates the Lord's aiśvaryam by mentioning the crown. Up to this point, the Āḻvār has described the avayava śobhai (beauty of individual divine parts). By 'tejas' (divine bodily effulgence or brilliance), the Āḻvār describes the samudāya śobhai (overall splendor of Śrī Raṅganātha). Āḻvār rhetorically asks how bhaktas can leave away all such beauties, which are here only for their enjoyment. He states that the beauty of the Lord is for devotees to enjoy, and that they are unable to leave such wealth, even if they are carried away by it.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh my destitute mind! answer me. Even the scriptures abound in the adorations of Him (Lord Raṅganātha), but they cannot fully encompass his supreme qualities. He cannot be known by the parviscient persons, because only men free from impurities can know Him. We should merely worship Him and be content with it; for, He rests only in the heart of persons with purity of mind. Is there anything we can say more about Him?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Alvar quotes again that how he is beyond the prakriti tattvas and hence no one can know him completly. Indeed his qualities and infinte and apar from our capability understand. Only he knows the Leelas he perform. The Taiterrya states aprāpya manasā saha .i.e even when the mind tried to reach him and understand Bhagavan, it returned baffled. But he resides in the heart of Yogis and devotees who have their mind free from impure thoughts just like Vishnu Sahasranama quotes it as yōgihṛddhyānagamyaṃ.

Hence, Alvar quotes that our mind is not capable of praising him when even Brahma, Rudra and other devatas could not praise the Supreme Lord. Hence, the best way for us to access him to chant his divine names and remember him. How else can we access him easily? Indeed there is nothing better than chainting his divine names.

docs.text: Tamil Transliteration கங்கையிற் புனித மாயகாவிரி நடுவு பாட்டு,பொங்குநீர் பரந்து பாயும்பூம்பொழி லரங்கந் தன்னுள்,எங்கள்மா லிறைவ னீசன்கிடந்ததோர் கிடக்கை கண்டும்,எங்ஙனம் மறந்து வாழ்கேன்ஏழையே னேழை யேனே kaṅgaiyin punidam āyakāviri naḍuvu pāṭṭupoṅgu nīr parandu pāyumpūm pozil araṅgan tannuḻeṅgaḻ māl iṟaivan īśankiḍandadōr kiḍakkai kaṇḍumeṅṅanam maṟandu vāzgēnēzaiyēn ēzaiyēnē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Could I forget Him and live? No. He is our supreme Lord, Tirumāl. I do look at His reclining posture as Śrī Raṅganātha. He dwells in the great Temple surrounded by the flowery groves watered by the holy river, Kāverī (Poṇṇi) which gushes forth and is more sacred than even the pure Ganges (Gaṅgā). When such is His great grace to be so nearer to our vision, am I to forget Him? If I could forget Him, then I should be poor, poor only.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The sacred Kāviri, surpassing even the holy Gaṅgā in purity, flows with divine grace. How does she excel? Not only in her enchanting beauty (darśanīyatā) and delightful presence (bhōgyatā), but most significantly, she cradles the reclining form of Śrī Raṅganātha Himself. While Gaṅgā once touched the Lord's feet, she later lost that honor, becoming 'raudram' as she fell from Śiva's matted locks. But Kāviri? She holds the very Lord who created Gaṅgā from His divine feet, much like Yaśōdā cradling Śrī Kṛṣṇa in her lap.

Behold how Kāviri, overjoyed at reaching Śrīraṅgam, spreads her waters with enthusiasm, embracing this holy place. Śrīraṅgam, a veritable paradise of blooming gardens (pūmpoḻil araṅgam), speaks of sanctity and tranquility. The abundance of water nourishes eternal spring, mirroring the Lord's eternal youthfulness (saukumāryam).

But why has our beloved Lord (eṅgaḷ māl) chosen this idyllic setting? Not for His comfort, but out of boundless love for His devotees. He is Iṟaivan, Īśan – the Supreme Lord to whom everything belongs, using all as He wills. And how He reclines! While others might appear ungainly in repose, Perumāḷ's reclining posture (kiṭanthatōr kiṭakkai) radiates unparalleled beauty.

Oh, how can one witness such splendor and continue to live in forgetfulness? Before beholding His sayanakōlam, life in saṃsāra might have been bearable. But now, having seen the Lord's magnificence, how can this lowly soul (ēḻaiyēṉ) ever forget? Alvar states he (we) lack the subtle mind to fully appreciate His presence, yet he (we) cannot bear His absence. Truly, He is (we) the most wretched (ēḻaiyēṉē), for how can he now live separated from such divine beauty?

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: O wretched mind! do you think you are strong? You are not ready to accept Him as the only supreme Master. It is quite strange that even though you have already perceived His charming lotus-like face, and you have also seen his enthralling reclining posture. He, the enticing Lord who rests at the Śrīraṅgam Temple girt with vast groves flooded by the sweet Kāverī waters, nevertheless you are shrewd and your devotion is, indeed, delusive. Alas, you are wasting your time cunningly.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The sacred Kāveri, born from the hallowed Sahyādri mountains, cascades with abundant waters and love through the lush gardens of Śrīraṅgam. Her devotion to the Lord is palpable as she approaches this divine abode, her waters spreading wide to embrace Śrī Raṅganātha in a tender aquatic embrace. But why does our Lord recline here? He is Kaḷvanār, the Divine Thief, who has descended to 'steal' away the misguided notion of independence from us saṃsārins, who have ourselves stolen our own ātmavastu.

Ah, but how cleverly He steals! Not through grand declarations that might incite resistance as in His Rāma and Kṛṣṇa avatāras, but through the simple, irresistible allure of His divine repose (kiṭanta āṟu). It is not His kalyāṇa guṇas or the beauty of His divine limbs that captivates us, but this exquisite reclining posture alone.

Behold His lotus-like countenance (kamala nal mukam)! Though we compare it to a lotus in bloom - its redness, fragrance, and coolness - His face surpasses even this noble flower. For while the lotus has its imperfections, the Lord's visage is eternally auspicious, pure sattva unmarred by material modes. It is jyotirmayam, radiant beyond compare, never diminishing, the sole eternal coolness in this fleeting saṃsāra.

Yet, oh our mind! (uḷḷamē)! How hard (valiyai) it remain! Even after witnessing such divine form (tirukkōlam) and countenance (tirumukha maṇḍalam), our mind fail to recognize Him as the One without second (oruvan eṉṟu uṇara māṭṭāy). Had you truly realized His advitīya nature, wouldn't you be consumed by an unquenchable thirst for bhagavad viṣayam?

Alas, the love we profess (kātal seytu) is but artificial (kaḷḷamē), a mere phalabhakti. Even in the presence of such paramabhāgyam, our devotion falls short of its exalted subject. While the Lord showers boundless love, while Kāveri flows with extraordinary devotion, my manas still fails to exhibit fitting bhakti. Oh, how we squander (kaḻikkiṉṟāyē) this precious opportunity in mere pretense (kaḷḷattē)!

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: I have thoroughly neglected Varṇāśrama dharma, the duties of caste and stage of life, viz. bathing thrice and adoring the three fires properly. I don't even look at them as my duties. Nor am I devoted to you. Oh Lord full of immense auspicious features! I have not done anything properly. How could I be pleased? O Lord of ocean-like blue colour! I am just crying aloud. O Lord of the great city, Srirangam! I beseech you, protect me and shower your ineffable grace on me.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār states that he does not have the capability to observe the rigorous rites meant for the three varṇika people. He declares himself incapable of adopting jñāna or bhakti yōgams to reach Him. The jñānam and bhakti, which the Āḻvār has shown until now, have come to him as bhagavat prasādam and helped him to enjoy the Lord. This jñānam and bhakti do not fall under the categories of jñāna yōgam and bhakti yōgam.

Āḻvār speaks of the many types of snānam (bathing) such as nitya snānam, naimittika snānam, prāyaścitta snānam, etc. He notes that one type of snānam does not represent the other and they differ for various occasions. He mentions the three sacred fires - gārhapatyam, āhavanīyam, and dakṣiṇāgni - that a brāhmaṇa must maintain. The Āḻvār compares a karmayōgi to a mother who always carries water and food for her weak child, always needing to carry firewood to maintain the fire. These, he says, are examples of the many rituals that must be strictly followed even before indulging in karmayōgam.

Āḻvār points out that even if one slip occurs while observing these rigorous rituals - be it mantralōpam, kriyālōpam, dravyalōpam, kālabhēdam - the ritual bears no fruit. "Karaṇam tappiṉāl maraṇam," says Periya Vachan Pillai. The Āḻvār confesses that apart from not having brāhmaṇyam, he also feigned Brahminism to the extent that the whole clan was belittled in society's eyes. This, he states, is the status of his karmayōgam. He declares that as karmayōgam is not relevant to him, jñāna yōgam is also irrelevant. Ātmāvalōkanam (sākṣātkāram of ātma) is also not possible for him. He recalls Śrī Yāmunācārya's stotra ratna verse: "na dharma niṣṭhōsmi na ca ātma vēdi na bhaktimān". He counters the argument that karmayōga anuṣṭhānam of a previous birth might have led to jñāna yōgam in this birth, stating that even that is not present in him. Āḻvār states that as he cannot even see his ātma, how can he meditate on the Lord. Thus, he is not a bhaktimān either. He declares that all three yōgās are not relevant to him, recalling the "nōṟṟa nōṉbilēṉ" and "kaṟavaigaḷ piṉseṉṟu" pāsurams.

Āḻvār admits he has no credits from any of these ways and is thus 'akiñcanan'. But he appeals to the Lord, who is guṇapūrṇan (repository of virtues), to save him. His appeal is similar to the Tiruppāvai pāsuram, where Śrī Āṇḍāḷ says "aṟivoṉṟum illātha āykulam" followed by "kuṟai oṉṟum illātha gōvindā". As in previous pāsurams where the Āḻvār described the Lord as "aiyappāḍu aṟuttu tōṉṟum aḻagaṉ" and "āḍaram peruga vaitta aḻagaṉ", here too he praises the Lord's beauty, comparing Him to the color of the sea. He states that he is only able to do maṅgaḷāśāsanam to the Lord's beauty. Although unworthy in other ways, he declares the Lord as his śaraṇyan (refuge).

Āḻvār pleads with the Lord to make him eligible for His grace and to grace him. The Āḻvār reminds the Lord that He has not come down to save blemishless people, but to save those without credits. He states that there can be no one more suitable than himself, as he looks only to the Lord. Although he has no credits, he depends solely on the Lord. He spends his time enjoying the Lord's divine beauty. He reminds the Lord that as the repository of all virtues, He must make the Āḻvār eligible for His grace and save him.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord of the great city, Śrirangam! I do not offer the fragrant flowers at the pair of your benign golden feet at any time. Nor do I praise you, delineating your auspicious qualities through the faultless words. Nor even am I devoted to you, heart and soul brimming with love. Therefore, you cannot count me as your own servant/devotee. Why have I been born? No purpose at all.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār laments his inability to worship the Lord properly. He states that while he had both eagerness and strength for worldly matters, he lacked these for divine service. He cites Viṣṇu Dharmam, which says only hands that worship Hari are true hands. The Āḻvār confesses to worshipping inappropriate things harmful to him in both saṃsāra and Śrī Vaikuṇṭha. He expresses his failure to praise the Lord's auspicious qualities with his speech, contrary to Viṣṇu Dharmam's teaching that the tongue praising Hari is the true tongue. The Āḻvār admits his tongue rolls easily for lowly matters but not for divine praise.

Regarding his heart, the Āḻvār confesses it hasn't shown true affection towards the Lord. He references Bhagavad Gītā to explain how worldly desires could be diverted towards the divine, but admits failing in this too. He cites Āḷavandār's Stotra Ratnam and Viṣṇu Purāṇam to illustrate his past insincere affections. The Āḻvār declares himself without anything (ēdhilēn) towards the Lord, who possesses all auspicious qualities as described in Stotra Ratnam. He laments losing the Lord not due to the Lord's distance or inappropriateness, but due to his own sin. Finally, the Āḻvār questions the purpose of his birth, stating that instead of using his God-given limbs for worship, he wasted them. He concludes that his birth, rather than benefiting anyone, has become a cause for many misdeeds for himself and others.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: O Lord Ranganatha! when the hosts of monkeys lifted up and carried hillocks for constructing a bund across the sea (in their service to Lord Rama), the small squirrel, free from deceit, transported particles of sand from the earth to the sea, by bathing in the sea first and rolling on the sands, and again bathing in the water of the sea. But, I am not like the squirrel free from malice. My mind is hard like the intractable trees. I am full of deceit in my heart. I do not carry out any service to You at all. Still I think that I am worthy of your grace. However, I do get lost myself.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text: The Āḻvār describes the scene of monkeys building the bridge to Laṅkā, emphasizing their eagerness to serve Rāma. He notes that many monkeys moved each mountain, showing their desire to participate in Rāma's service. He then speaks of the squirrels' contribution, who, seeing the monkeys' work as insufficient, decided to help. The squirrels would wet themselves in the ocean, roll in sand, and shake it off between the mountains. The Āḻvār admires their selfless service (salam ilā), contrasting it with his own lack of such devotion. The Āḻvār laments that his heart is as hard as trees, which unlike iron, cannot be shaped even when heated. He confesses to being deceitful, putting on an act of devotion while lacking true involvement in the Lord's matters. He admits to not serving the Lord with his heart as the squirrels did, despite the Lord valuing even small acts done with good intentions. The Āḻvār expresses sorrow at his failure to perform continuous service as expected of the ātmā. Finally, the Āḻvār states that he has forgotten the Lord and become useless, not due to distance from the Lord or lack of qualification, but due to his own forgetfulness. He references Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār's words to emphasize this point.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: The Lord of glittering effulgence, unknown to Brahmā, Śiva and other gods, came out swiftly in anger, against the crocodile which lives on bloody flesh, to protect the elephant (ready to offer the lotus flower by his trunk). Are we able to save ourselves from any burden? No. We are merely dogs. We don't realise our meekness. Without doing service to our supreme Lord Ranganātha, for what purpose have I been born at all?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār humbly acknowledges his inability to observe the rigorous rites prescribed for the three varṇika people. He confesses his incapacity to adopt jñāna or bhakti yōgams as means to reach the Lord. The jñānam and bhakti that the Āḻvār has exhibited thus far have come to him as bhagavat prasādam, enabling him to relish the Lord's divine beauty. It is important to note that this jñānam and bhakti do not fall under the categories of jñāna yōgam and bhakti yōgam.

The Āḻvār eloquently speaks of the various types of snānam (ritual bathing) such as nitya snānam, naimittika snānam, and prāyaścitta snānam. He observes that each type of snānam serves a distinct purpose and differs for various occasions. He reverently mentions the three sacred fires - gārhapatyam, āhavanīyam, and dakṣiṇāgni - that a brāhmaṇa must diligently maintain.

Drawing a poignant comparison, the Āḻvār likens a karmayōgi to a devoted mother who constantly carries water and food for her weak child, always needing to gather firewood to maintain the sacred fire. These, he explains, exemplify the numerous rituals that must be meticulously followed even before embarking on karmayōgam. With great humility, the Āḻvār points out that even a single lapse in observing these rigorous rituals - be it mantralōpam, kriyālōpam, dravyalōpam, or kālabhēdam - renders the ritual fruitless. As Periya Vachan Pillai wisely states, "Karaṇam tappiṉāl maraṇam" (a mistake in performance leads to spiritual death).

The Āḻvār candidly confesses that not only does he lack true brāhmaṇyam, but he has also feigned Brahminism to such an extent that his entire clan has been belittled in society's eyes. This, he laments, is the pitiful state of his karmayōgam. He humbly declares that as karmayōgam is irrelevant to him, so too is jñāna yōgam. Ātmāvalōkanam (direct perception of the self) is also beyond his reach.

Recalling Śrī Yāmunācārya's profound words from the stotra ratna, "na dharma niṣṭhōsmi na ca ātma vēdi na bhaktimān" (I am neither steadfast in dharma, nor a knower of the self, nor filled with devotion), the Āḻvār aligns himself with this sentiment. He refutes the notion that karmayōga anuṣṭhānam from a previous birth might have led to jñāna yōgam in this life, stating that even this is absent in him.

The Āḻvār humbly admits that as he cannot even perceive his own ātma, how can he hope to meditate on the Lord? Thus, he acknowledges that he is not a bhaktimān either. He declares with profound honesty that all three yōgās are beyond his reach, echoing his earlier sentiments expressed in the pāsurams "nōṟṟa nōṉbilēṉ" and "kaṟavaigaḷ piṉseṉṟu".

Acknowledging his lack of spiritual credits, the Āḻvār humbly admits to being 'akiñcanan' (one who has nothing). Yet, he fervently appeals to the Lord, who is guṇapūrṇan (the repository of all virtues), to save him. His heartfelt plea resonates with Śrī Āṇḍāḷ's words in Tiruppāvai: "aṟivoṉṟum illātha āykulam" followed by "kuṟai oṉṟum illātha gōvindā".

As in previous pāsurams where the Āḻvār reverently described the Lord as "aiyappāḍu aṟuttu tōṉṟum aḻagaṉ" and "āḍaram peruga vaitta aḻagaṉ", here too he extols the Lord's beauty, likening Him to the majestic hue of the sea. He humbly states that he is only capable of offering maṅgaḷāśāsanam (auspicious praises) to the Lord's divine beauty. Though unworthy in other respects, he wholeheartedly declares the Lord as his śaraṇyan (ultimate refuge).

With deep devotion, the Āḻvār implores the Lord to make him worthy of His grace and to bestow His blessings upon him. He gently reminds the Lord that His divine purpose is not to save the already blemishless, but to redeem those without spiritual credits. The Āḻvār humbly suggests that there can be no one more suitable for the Lord's grace than himself, as he looks solely to the Lord for salvation.

Though bereft of spiritual merits, the Āḻvār's unwavering dependence on the Lord and his constant contemplation of the Lord's divine beauty serve as his only solace. He respectfully reminds the Lord that as the repository of all virtues, it is incumbent upon Him to make the Āḻvār eligible for His grace and to ultimately save him from the cycle of saṃsāra.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: I don't belong to any sacred place; nor do I possess any acre of land; nor even do I have any kinsmen; on this earth, I have not even any trace of devotion towards the sole of the pair of your feet. Oh supreme Lord! O lustrous Lord of rain-cloud- hue! O Lord Kṛṣṇa of enticing beauty! prithee, I do cry aloud. Who else is there to weed out my difficulties other than You? Oh Lord of the great city, Śrirangam!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The "ūr" (town) that the Āḻvār refers to here is not any ordinary town. He speaks of divya dēśams where emperumāṉ eternally resides, such as Śrī Sālagrāmam, Śrī Rāma's birthplace Ayodhyā, and Śrīraṅgam (Thiruvaraṅgam), the foremost of all arcāvatāra sthalams. How can the term "ūr" refer to divya dēśam? It does so due to the context of this particular section of Thirumālai, which deals with the Āḻvār's ākiñcanyam - his utter helplessness in attaining emperumāṉ. Since he states "ūrilēṉ", the term "ūr" must signify a path to mōkṣam. As there is no sentient being who is not born in a town, if "ūr" were to refer to any town, then all towns would become means to attain mōkṣam. There is no authoritative source to support such an interpretation. Thus, considering various authentic sources, one must conclude that "ūr" refers specifically to divya dēśam. The Āḻvār humbly admits, "Had I been born in a divya dēśam, You would have endeavored to rescue me, as I would have been born in a place that gives You joy. Alas, I do not even have that to my credit." Is there evidence to suggest that residing in a divya dēśam can lead to one's salvation? Indeed, there are many. The Gāruḍa Purāṇam 11 states: "dēśo'yam sarvakāma duk" (this place confers everything). Śrī Rāmāyaṇa, Āraṇya Kāṇḍam 1.20 declares: "tē vayaṁ bhavatā rakṣyā bhavat viṣaya vāsinaḥ" (we, who dwell and suffer in Your domain, are to be protected by You) [thus speak the ṛṣis of Daṇḍakāraṇyam to Śrī Rāma]. Śrī Rāmāyaṇa, Uttara Kāṇḍam 109.22 proclaims: "nocchvasat tadayodhyāyāṁ susūkṣmamapi dṛśyatē | tiryak yoni gatāścānyē sarvē rāmānuvratāḥ ||" (Not even the tiniest creature remains alive in Ayodhyā. All beings, including animals, have followed Śrī Rāma [to Paramapadam]). Thus, numerous authoritative sources confirm this.

"Even if you were not born in a divya dēśam, perhaps you have some connection through landed property. Do you possess such a link?" asks emperumāṉ. The Āḻvār humbly responds that he lacks even that. In bygone days, land was often gifted or leased for performing kainkaryams to emperumāṉ, such as reciting Tiruppallāṇḍu in the temple or creating gardens for stringing flower garlands for Him. The Āḻvār confesses that he lacks this connection as well. Emperumāṉ inquires further, "Even if you lack a connection through birth or landed property with a divya dēśam, do you have any association through people there with whom you exchange gifts or through mantras (either learning or teaching)?" The Āḻvār replies that he has no relatives there, thus no connection with divya dēśam. By saying "no one," he emphasizes the absence of even distant relatives he might have occasionally encountered or friends with whom he might have had some association - there is absolutely no one, the Āḻvār laments. In that case, where does the Āḻvār reside?

The Āḻvār states that he dwells on this earth, which creates boundless difficulties for those without a place to stay. He contrasts this with Śrīvaikuṇṭham, described in Mūṉṟām Tiruvandhādhi 51 as "kalaṅgāp perunagaram" (the trouble-free great abode). In Śrīvaikuṇṭham, one can live without worry, free from the afflictions of lust, anger, and other vices. On this earth, however, seven people vie for the food and clothing meant for one person. "I am living in such a wretched place," the Āḻvār laments. "I have no connection with Your divine feet, which offer refuge to those who have nowhere else to turn," confesses the Āḻvār. Niṉ pādhamūlam - Śrī Rāmāyaṇa, Sundara Kāṇḍam 38.33 states: "sa pitrā ca parityaktas suraiśca sa maharṣibhiḥ | trīn lokān samparikramya tamēva śaraṇaṁ gataḥ ||" (Kākāsuran, abandoned by his father, mother, celestial beings, and sages, traversed all three worlds before finally seeking refuge at Śrī Rāma's feet). The Āḻvār expresses his deep anguish at being unworthy to seek refuge under emperumāṉ's divine feet, which granted sanctuary even to Kākāsuran, who had committed an intolerable offense and became the target of His brahmāstra. Periya Perumāḷ then tells him, "If you have no benefit in any way, it seems there is no alternative but to forfeit the opportunity of attaining Me."

The Āḻvār responds, "I have nothing to protect myself. But don't You have the means to protect me? You possess boundless resources. Aren't You the Lord of all, far above everyone else? Only by protecting me too can You truly be the Lord of all. If You do not protect a śēṣabhūtan (a devoted follower), You cannot be a śēṣi (the Supreme Lord). For that to occur, shouldn't a śēṣabhūtan realize his servitude?" The sentiment here is that even when the sentient being, in a state of delusion, believes himself to be independent, sarvēśvaran, considering Himself the owner and the sentient being His possession, will correct the being and make him realize the true relationship between them.

Emperumāṉ asks the Āḻvār, "Since it is undeniable that you are My servitor, what is the means for you to attain that servitorship?" To which the Āḻvār responds that His divine beauty is the means. Kāroḷi vaṇṇaṉē - In pāsuram 16, the Āḻvār had said "ādharam perugavaitta aḻagaṉ" (the beautiful form of emperumāṉ that engenders affection). Emperumāṉ initially kindles interest towards Himself in the mind of the sentient being. Once this interest is awakened, His form (beauty) becomes the means for the being to attain Him. When that beauty resides in emperumāṉ, there is no obstacle for the Āḻvār to obtain servitorship, he declares.

Even if the form is beautiful, instead of remaining in Śrīvaikuṇṭham where You could not be reached, You made Yourself accessible to us by taking various incarnations and exhibiting auspicious qualities such as saulabhyam (simplicity). Since You are parama mūrtti, You are our incomparable Lord; since You are kāroḷi vaṇṇaṉ, You create in us, as upāyam (means), everything beginning with desire; since You are Kaṇṇaṉ, You possess auspicious qualities such as simplicity and affability. With all these attributes, how can I fail to achieve my goal? You are the perfect Lord for us all. Even if You were not the Lord, Your beauty is such that we cannot ignore You. Even if You lacked these two great qualities, You possess auspicious qualities like simplicity and affability, and You associate closely with us. With such an entity as You present, I have no deficiency. Kadhaṟugiṉṟēṉ - When I contemplate such greatness in You, I cry out to You, just as those who observe other means such as bhakti cry out when there is a delay in attaining You.

Are You delaying in protecting me when I cry out to You because You think someone else will protect me? Can I protect myself with nothing in my possession? Can someone else, who doesn't know as well as I do that I have nothing, protect me? If the possession is destroyed, is it not a loss to You, the Owner? Even if You are the owner, if You were not near me, I might have remained calm, using that as an excuse. The meaning here is that "when You are reclining in the nearby temple [at Śrīraṅgam], anticipating whether someone will come calling out to You to attain You, how can I remain silent and not cry out to You?"

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Neither I have purity of mind, nor do I utter amicable words. Angrily I am always expressing the burning words of insult (to one and all), without any cause whatsoever. O Lord adorned with fragrant Tulasi garlands! O sacred Lord of Srirangam, girt with the great river Ponni (Kāvēri)! You are the supreme Lord who have myself as your dependent. Kindly tell me, henceforth, what is the way left for me to reach the supreme goal.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
"Na cakṣuṣā gṛhyatē nāpi vācā manasā tu viśuddhēna" (The Supreme Self cannot be apprehended by the eyes or speech; only through a purified mind can He be realized). Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇam 1.4.41 declares: "yē tu jñānavidhaḥ śuddha cētasastē'khilaṁ jagat | jñānātmakaṁ prapaśyanti tvad rūpaṁ paramēśvara" (O Paramēśvara! Those who realize that the Self is of the nature of knowledge and possess purified minds perceive the entire world as permeated with knowledge and as Your body). Thus, the śāstras affirm that purity of mind is considered a means for experiencing paramātmajñānam (knowledge of the Supreme Self).

The Āḻvār humbly confesses that he lacks even this purity of mind. By saying "ōr tūymai", he indicates that he lacks even the slightest purity one might attain if any of the mind's impurities such as kāmam (lust), kōpam (anger), lōbham (greed), bhayam (fear), dvēṣam (hatred), madam (arrogance), mōham (delusion), and mātsaryam (envy) were diminished. By stating "tūymai illai", he emphasizes that it is not a matter of his mind being occasionally muddled and occasionally pure. Rather, he asserts that he is perpetually devoid of mental purity. There is no purity of mind, granted. But at least, through speech, is there the virtue of uttering sweet words? The Āḻvār laments that he lacks even this. By saying "ōr iṉsol illai", he confesses that he has never inquired about another's well-being, which could be pleasing to their ears. He intimates that even when others inquire about his well-being, he has not responded kindly. Just as Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār said in Periya Tirumoḻi 1.6.5, "neḍuñ collāl maṟutta nīcaṉēṉ" (I am a lowly person who rebuked with harsh words), this Āḻvār echoes the same sentiment. By using "ōr", he hints that even in conversations with those he loves, he uses only harsh words that sear their ears. Thus, with these two phrases, he succinctly expresses what he had elaborated in the previous five pāsurams. From this point onward, for the remainder of the pāsuram, he speaks of his negative qualities.

Even if he lacked purity of mind and sweetness of speech, others could distance themselves from him and carry on. But he does not stop there. He voluntarily approaches a person of some greatness and, without reason, causes them harm. Initially, he displays all the anger in his mind and looks at them with hostility. "Seṟṟam nōkki" means to look with enmity. Alternatively, since both "seṟṟam" and "siṉam" indicate anger, their combined use here signifies intense anger. The implication is that his fiery gaze would almost cause the other person to collapse under the weight of his wrath. It is not only through looks; even the words he uses would seem like burning embers to the other person, causing them to wither completely. Is the purpose of all this to gain anything?

These actions are not performed in anticipation of any benefit. Looking at someone with anger and scolding them with harsh words become sources of enjoyment in themselves. No other benefit is needed for such actions. The sentiment here is that just as virtuous persons consider doing good to others as inherently beneficial, the Āḻvār regards harming others as inherently rewarding to himself. Periya Perumāḷ says that since he is such a reprehensible person, there would be no benefit in compelling him. The Āḻvār responds:

Sentient beings cannot abandon Him after recognizing their own lowliness because He has pledged to protect them if they desire Him. He wears a garland of tuḷasī to openly display this quality. The meaning here is that since You are the ordained Lord and after perceiving Your sweetness, how can I let go of You? "Puṉam" refers to the land where the tuḷasī plant flourishes. The tuḷasī on His chest thrives as it would in its native soil, and He wears such a garland. Even if You are a protector, if You are not near me, it will not benefit me. Only to ensure that even the lowliest can attain You, You have come to Śrīraṅgam and assumed a reclining posture here. This is my good fortune, the Āḻvār feels. "Poṉṉi sūḻ" - atop the tuḷasī garland, the holy Kāvēri surrounding Him is like another garland.

To me, with all the lowliness that has been described thus far. Considering my unworthiness, I cannot protect myself, and after entrusting the responsibility of protecting me to You, Please show me the path to my salvation. Even after accumulating all these faults such that it seems impossible to uplift himself, the Āḻvār can still plead his case with Him for upliftment because emperumāṉ is the ordained Lord. "What compels Me to show you the way to your salvation?" asks emperumāṉ. You being the svāmi (Lord) and I being the servitor are eternal states. Hence, who else can protect me? If my ātmavastu (the entity called ātmā) were to degrade, wouldn't the shortcoming due to that be Yours?

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord of the great temple town, Srirangam! I don't belong to any one group of the aspirants; nor do I belong to the wealthy class; I am, indeed, nothing worth the name even to my relatives, i.e., I am like brackish water (of slums); enticed by the rosy lips of damsels, I have become a knave. O Lord Ranganatha! You have merely given me a lease of life that I spend in vain.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār laments his spiritual inadequacy, confessing that he did not engage in tapas (penance) for attaining mokṣa. He cites the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.22, which states that brahma jñānis seek to know Paramātmā through Vedic recitation, rituals, donations, and desireless penance. The Āḻvār admits he neither joined those who performed penance for mokṣa nor those who sought svarga (heaven). He even distanced himself from those who, upon realizing shortcomings in their penance, made atonements.

Regarding wealth, the Āḻvār confesses he was not among those who earned money for noble purposes, as prescribed in the Bhagavad Gītā 18.5 and 17.20. He acknowledges the Taittirīya Upaniṣad's directive to earn wealth even through questionable means if it's for hosting guests, but admits he failed to follow this path.

The Āḻvār expresses his inability to be of any use to his relatives, comparing himself to salty water that causes discomfort. He confesses to causing harm to his kin, bringing shame upon himself. Even towards women, whom he should have treated with affection, he behaved poorly, becoming a thief (thurisan) of their trust.

Addressing Raṅganātha, the Lord of Śrīraṅgam, the Āḻvār laments the apparent waste of his birth (avattamē piṟavi tandāy). He acknowledges that his karma led to his lowly state but doesn't blame the Lord, understanding that both his actions and inactions are under divine control. The Āḻvār alludes to the Bhagavad Gītā 10.10, recognizing that if the Lord chose to grant him good intelligence, nothing could prevent it.

Finally, the Āḻvār points out that despite the Lord's presence in Śrīraṅgam (Araṅga mā nagar) to guide those lost in worldly pursuits, this divine grace did not seem to fructify in his case. This poignant confession reflects the Āḻvār's deep introspection and his yearning for spiritual redemption.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord Kṛṣṇa of charming beauty like the dense dark rainy clouds! You are dwelling as Śri Ranganatha at Srirangam beautified by the surrounding groves resounding with the humming of honey-bees. I am only a knave among human beings because I do not know the right path to perceive You in the proper perspective. Though I have come (seeking you), nevertheless I am just a wicked, and wicked alone.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār describes the scene in Śrīraṅgam, where beetles, intoxicated by excess honey from the lush groves, buzz and wander aimlessly. He likens their state to that of muktas (liberated souls) in Paramapada, who sing Sāma Gāna out of sheer joy after experiencing the Lord. This comparison elevates the sweetness of Śrīraṅgam to that of the divine realm.

Drawing a parallel to the Rāmāyaṇa's Sundara Kāṇḍa, where monkeys celebrate in Madhuvana after sighting Sītā, the Āḻvār notes a distinction: while he cries out for existence, the beetles cry out of joy. The phrase "vaṇḍu alambum sōlai" likens the beetles' predicament to Mārkaṇḍeya Maharṣi tossed in the great deluge, emphasizing the overwhelming nature of Śrīraṅgam's beauty.

Śrīraṅgam is described as "aṇi araṅgam", an ornament to saṃsāra. The Āḻvār alludes to Rāmāyaṇa, where a husband is considered a woman's greatest ornament, to highlight Raṅganātha's significance to the world. The Lord's form, "kārttiraḷ anaiya mēni", is compared to rain-laden clouds, not just in color but in qualities of coolness and selfless giving. The term "Kaṇṇan" is used to emphasize His accessibility, contrasting with the distant nature of clouds.

The Āḻvār laments his ignorance of the paths to attain the Lord, despite being born human. He calls himself "thurisanāya" (a thief or cheat), suggesting that compared to him, others might seem like nitya sūris (eternal devotees). Finally, addressing his audacity in approaching the Lord, the Āḻvār describes himself as "mūrkkan" (a fool), repeating it for emphasis. He acknowledges his ignorance of both the Lord's greatness and his own lowliness, likening his approach to poisoning the pure water enjoyed by the wise. This passage beautifully intertwines devotional fervor with self-deprecation, using rich imagery and scriptural references to convey the Āḻvār's spiritual struggle and deep reverence for Raṅganātha.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord! O Śri Ranganatha! I have completely abandoned truthfulness on thought, word and deed. I have been ensnared by damsels of beautiful locks of hair, and I have experienced untold miseries. I am a shameless person abounding in falsehood, and falsehood alone. Though I am falsehood incarnate, I have come to You, with the desire to obtain your grace. Nevertheless, I spoke untruth; even now, I am only untruthful.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār discusses the concept of mey (truth), defining it as that which leads to good for all jīvātmās and describes things as they are. He cites the Kaiśika Māhātmyam, where Nampāduvān declares the primacy of truth in sustaining the world.

The Āḻvār confesses, "ellām pōgaviṭṭu" (I got rid of all truths), implying he lacks truthfulness even towards relatives. He laments speaking lies to the omniscient Lord Himself. When questioned about the source of his deceit, the Āḻvār attributes it to his association with women: "viri kuḻalāril paṭṭu" (entangled with women of flowing hair). He elaborates on how impossible it is to speak truth in women's company, comparing it to the impossibility of lying in the Lord's presence. Āḻvār describes himself as a repository of falsehoods, contrasting with his earlier renunciation of all truths. Addressing himself as "pōtkanēn" (one without refuge), the Āḻvār stands before the Lord despite his unworthiness, drawn by their inseverable relationship. He refers to the Lord as "Aiyane" and "Araṅgane", acknowledging this bond and the Lord's presence in Śrīraṅgam.

The Āḻvār expresses his desire for the Lord's grace: "un aruḷ eṉṉum āsai taṉṉāl vantu niṉṟēṉ" (I came standing with the desire for your grace). He cites the Rāmāyaṇa to illustrate the Lord's compassion even towards the undeserving. Finally, the Āḻvār admits that even his confession might be false: "poyyaṉēṉ poyyaṉēṉē" (I am a liar, indeed a liar). He references the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā, suggesting that acknowledging one's faults before the Lord can yield benefits. However, he questions the sincerity of his own admission, wondering how many lies he can tell in the divine presence where only truth should be spoken. This passage beautifully captures the Āḻvār's deep introspection, his struggle with truthfulness, and his complex relationship with the divine, all expressed through rich scriptural allusions and poetic imagery.
