docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration உள்ளத்தே உறையும்‌ மாலை.உள்ளுவான்‌ உணர்வொன்றில்லாக்‌ ,கள்ளத்தேன்‌ நானும்‌ தொண்டாய்த்‌,தொண்டுக்கே கோலம்‌ பூண்டு.உள்ளுவார்‌ உள்ளிற்றெல்லாம்‌,உடன்‌ இருந்தறிதி என்று .வெள்கிப்போய்‌ என்னுள்ளே நான்‌,விலவறச்‌ சிரித்திட்டேனே ! uḻḻattē uṟaiyum mālaiuḻḻuvān uṇarvonṟillākaḻḻattēn nānum toṇḍāytoṇḍukkē kōlam pūṇḍuuḻḻuvār uḻḻiṭrellāmuḍan irundaṟidi enṟuveḻgippōy ennuḻḻē nānvilavaṟa ccirittiṭṭēnē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord Ranganatha! You are dwelling in the heart of everyone and affectionate towards all creatures. I do not have adequate knowledge even to contemp late upon You. However, I am a deceitful person. I pose my- self as your servant and so, put on the guise of doing service under You; when I am able to recognize that You are the in-dweller, and so you are capable of gleaning the thought (idea) of every- one, being ever a companion - I feel quite ashamed and even then, I abandon You (i.e. move off from your holy shrine), and so laugh at myself as my ribs could break into pieces within my heart where, indeed, You hid yourself.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār contemplates the omnipresence of Emperumān, particularly His dwelling in the heart (uṟaiyum), the springboard of thoughts. He emphasizes the impossibility of deceiving the Lord, who is described as Mālai (the supreme one), knowing and controlling everything. The Āḻvār laments his lack of spiritual knowledge: "uḷḷuvān uṇarvu illā" (without the knowledge to meditate on His indwelling presence). He confesses to having no understanding of either the jīvātmā or Paramātmā, nor of the body's transient nature. Calling himself "kaḷḷattēṉ" (a thief), the Āḻvār admits to deceiving both the foolish and the learned by feigning ignorance or humility. He acknowledges the impropriety of his attempts at service (toṇḍu), citing Śrī Rāmāyaṇa to illustrate the despicable nature of one unseen by Rāma.

Āḻvār confesses to wearing the external symbols of devotion (Ūrdhva puṇḍras, divine weapons) and reciting divine names without true belief, misleading others about his spiritual status. The realization dawns: "uḷḷuvār uḷḷiṟṟellām uḍaṉ irundu aṟidi eṉṟu" (You know all thoughts of those who think). The Āḻvār references Śakuntalā's words to Duṣyanta from the Mahābhārata, highlighting the futility of deceit before the omniscient Lord.

Overcome with shame (veḷgip pōy), the Āḻvār attempts to flee the Lord's presence, only to realize the impossibility of finding a place devoid of His presence. This realization leads to self-deprecating laughter (eṉṉuḷḷē nāṉ viḷavaṟac cirittiṭṭēṉē), so intense that his ribs metaphorically break. The passage concludes by comparing the Āḻvār's attempt to leave Emperumān's presence to one adorning oneself before committing suicide, highlighting the absurdity of trying to escape the omnipresent divine. This poignant self-realization is juxtaposed with Arjuna's moment of despair in the Bhagavad Gītā, emphasizing the Āḻvār's spiritual crisis and the profound understanding of the inescapable nature of the divine presence.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh! my supreme Lord who have encompassed all the worlds, without leaving any space, when You begged the great emperor, Mahābali, and got the three foot-steps of space from him! I am sure I won't bow to any other god except You. Oh! graceful Lord with reddish lotus-like eyes! Oh my supreme Self! Oh nectarine immortal Lord! Oh beneficent Lord similar to my rare life-birth! I will never think of any important goal other than You. Though I deem myself sinful, I do, again, sinful deeds alone.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The Āḻvār expresses his deep regret at emperumāṉ's unanticipated act of placing His divine foot upon the heads of saṃsārīs. He reflects that had emperumāṉ forewarned of His intention, the saṃsārīs, burdened with immense ego, would have refused this divine grace, commanding Him, "Do not place Your foot upon us." Just as those of sattva guṇa would have beseeched, "thiruvāṇai niṉṉāṇai" (Thiruvāimoḻi 10.10.2) to ensure emperumāṉ's divine foot rested upon their heads, these saṃsārīs would have vehemently opposed His approach. It was for this reason that emperumāṉ, in His infinite wisdom, placed His foot upon their heads without their knowledge, growing rapidly in form without causing fatigue to either Himself or the saṃsārīs.

On that day when the hierarchy between master and servitor lay in ruins, and Mahābali had seized the worlds. Not content with merely measuring the three worlds seized by Mahābali, His divine foot extended to Brahmalōka, after gracing the heads of all beings without discrimination, expanding in size. Āḻvār illustrates that the protector's [emperumāṉ's] excitement surpassed the magnitude of what He protected. The Puruṣa Sūktam 1 proclaims, "sahasra śīrṣā puruṣa: sahasrākṣa: sahasrapādh | sa bhūmim viśvathō vruthvā athyathiṣṭadhdhaśāṅgulam ||" (Nārāyaṇa, known as Puruṣa, possesses countless heads, eyes, and legs; He encompassed the earth on all sides and pervaded countless yōjanas beyond).

Āḻvār addresses emperumāṉ thus, recognizing that His divine feet, described by Thirumangai Āḻvār in Thirukkuṟundhāṇḍagam 6 as "amarar seṉṉippūviṉai" (the divine feet borne by nityasūris on their heads), had also graced his own head on that day. The Āḻvār reflects that it is due to the merit of that encounter that he has attained enlightenment today. He declares, "Having realized Your simplicity, I shall not depart from You hereafter, nor cling to anything else." He affirms that he will neither seek independence like a king nor become a servitor to another, echoing the essence of the Thirumanthram [aṣṭākṣaram]. Āḻvār assures emperumāṉ that his determination will last eternally, until his ātmā ceases to exist. Like Nammāḻvār in Thiruvāimoḻi 2.6.1, he offers solace to emperumāṉ, who grieves at the thought of the Āḻvār's departure. This epithet reflects not just the natural redness of emperumāṉ's eyes but the unique radiance acquired upon hearing the Āḻvār's declaration of eternal devotion. The Āḻvār, like Hanumān in the Rāmāyaṇa, offers refuge to periya perumāḷ in His archāvatāram, assuring Him of his unwavering devotion

docs.text: Tamil Transliteration மழைக்கன்று வரை முன்‌ ஏந்தும்‌மைந்தனே ! மதுர ஆறேஉழைக்கன்றே போலநோக்கம்‌ உடையவர்‌ வலையுள்‌ பட்டுஉழைக்கின்றேற்குஎன்னை நோக்காதொழிவதேஉன்னை அன்றே அழைக்கின்றேன்‌ ஆதி மூர்த்தி !அரங்க மா நகருளானே ! mazaikkanṟu varai mun ēndummaindanē ! madura āṟēuzaikkanṟē pōlanōkkam uḍaiyavar valaiyuḻ paṭṭuuzaikkinṟēṟkuennai nōkkādozivadēunnai anṟē azaikkinṟēn ādi mūrtti !araṅga mā nagaruḻānē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh! primeval supreme Being! Lord of the great city, Śrirangam! Oh sweet flow of bountiful compassion! Oh Lord of fresh youth (Śrī Kṛṣṇa) in which you lifted aloft on your little finger the mount Govardhana, for the Make of protecting the cowherds and Gokula (Āyarpāḍi) from the fury of Indra's torrential stony rain! Why are you going away without looking at me who am bound in the net of the doe eyed damsels? I do call You, Oh! supreme Lord!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Among the Āḻvārs, whenever they employ the term "maḻai" [rain], it invariably alludes to the hailstones that Indra [lord of celestial entities] showered when Kṛṣṇa lifted the Gōvardhan mountain, just as the word "āṉai" [elephant] always refers to Gajēndrāḻvāṉ [the elephant caught by the crocodile when it entered the pond to pluck a flower for emperumāṉ]. The Āḻvār now invokes the prevention of hailstones by lifting Gōvardhana mountain to illustrate his yearning to attain Him and overcome the sorrows of saṃsāra (materialistic realm). He recalls how the cowherds overcame the dangers posed by Indra by seeking refuge in Him. Just as the hungry call out to the wealthy, "Oh Lord! Please remove our hunger," the Āḻvār beseeches emperumāṉ, "Oh One who rids people of dangers! Please remove my peril."

The Śrīviṣṇu Purāṇam 5.11.13 states, "thathasthath gōkulam sarvam gōgōpījanasaṅkulam | athīvārththam harir dhṛṣṭvā maithrēyāchinthayath thadhā ||" (Oh Maitreya! Upon seeing the entire Gōkulam, full of cows and gōpīkās, in sorrow, [Kṛṣṇa] immediately began to ponder). Aṉṟu refers to the day when the calves, cows, and cowherds trembled at the sight of Indra's hailstones. The Āḻvār equates his present danger to that faced by the inhabitants of Gōkulam, beseeching emperumāṉ for protection from his shower of sorrow. When Indra commanded all clouds to open, they poured with such intensity that it resembled the great deluge. Seeing Indra's wrath for being denied food by Āyppādi, Kṛṣṇa, without time to summon His Sudarśana Chakra, lifted the nearest mountain. The Āḻvār infers that emperumāṉ cannot claim lack of suitable means to offer protection.

Having already used "aṉṟu" to denote a specific time, "muṉ" here signifies "before harm befell the cows." The Āḻvār emphasizes that emperumāṉ did not wait for harm to come to the cows and cowherds but protected them preemptively, as they had no other refuge. Āḷavandhār, in his Stōtra Ratnam 49, similarly beseeches, "avivēkaghanāndhathingmukhē bahudhā santhathadhu:kha varṣiṇi | bhagavan! bhavadhurthdhinē padha: skalitham māmavalōkayāchutha! ||" The Āḻvār marvels at how Kṛṣṇa effortlessly lifted the mountain at merely seven years of age, as if it were a garland of flowers. He questions whether emperumāṉ's reluctance to protect him stems from a fear of fatigue.

Oh One of immense strength to lift a mountain! Alternatively, maindhaṉ indicates youthfulness, suggesting One who becomes young in spirit upon protecting His devotees. The Āḻvār laments that while protecting him benefits emperumāṉ, he must still call out for protection. Oh One who is like a river of sweetness! Even if You were not the protector but one who might chastise the devotee, Your beauty is such that none would forsake You. The Āḻvār likens emperumāṉ to a river rather than a sea, for river water proves useful for bathing on a hot day, washing one's face, or quenching thirst. Like a flowing river during floods, this loving river [emperumāṉ] gushes in, breaking the dam of unworthiness the Āḻvār had built around himself.

The Āḻvār, trapped in the net of women's fawn-like eyes, laments his suffering. These women, though devoid of genuine affection, feign devotion, ensnaring him with their deceptive gazes. He pleads, "ennai nōkkādhu oḻivadhē" – why do You not look upon me (protect me)? The Āḻvār's closeness to emperumāṉ and the latter's affability allow him to express such sadness. The Āḻvār reminds emperumāṉ of His responsibility as the creator, citing the Chāndōgya Upaniṣad 6.2.9, "thadhaikṣatha bahu syām prajāyēyēthi thath thējō'sṛjatha" (That Brahman took a vow "I will multiply myself" and created radiance).

The Āḻvār questions the need to seek protection at the origin of creation when emperumāṉ has already descended to Śrīraṅgam. He implores, "After You came to Śrīraṅgam to cultivate a taste for righteousness, and after I acquired that taste, should I lose it?" Even as the Āḻvār calls out, emperumāṉ remains silent, savoring the long-awaited sincere devotion. The efforts He had taken since time immemorial are now bearing fruit, and He wishes to hear the Āḻvār's earnest plea a while longer before responding.

docs.text: Tamil Transliteration தெளிவிலாக்‌ கலங்கல்‌ நீர்‌ சூழ்‌திருவரங்கத்துள்‌ ஓங்கும்‌ஒளி உளார்‌ தாமே அன்றேதந்தையும்‌ தாயும்‌ ஆவார்‌எளியதோர்‌ அருளும்‌ அன்றேஎன்‌ திறத்தெம்‌ பிரானார்‌அளியன்‌ நம்‌ பையல்‌ என்னார்‌அம்மவோ ! கொடியவாறே ! teḻivilā kkalaṅgal nīr śūztiruvaraṅgattuḻ ōṅgumoḻi uḻār tāmē anṟētandaiyum tāyum āvāreḻiyadōr aruḻum anṟēen tiṟattem pirānāraḻiyan nam paiyal ennārammavō ! koḍiyavāṟē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: The supreme Lord of great splendour dwelling in the lofty shrine of Srirangam which is surrounded by the agitated muddy waters (of the holy river Kāvēri), indeed, is our father and mother. Would He not ward off my anguish, by showering His ineffable grace on me, after saying "This pitiable fellow is, indeed, my boy worthy of my blessings"? But, He has not yet blessed me. Alas! what a cruelty of fate!

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
As the flow of water in Kāvēri eases, it gains clarity. Yet, with increasing floods, it remains perpetually muddied. Similarly, this Āḻvār, like Kāvēri, is in constant agitation. Before attaining emperumāṉ, he frets, "I have not attained Him." Upon attainment, he becomes agitated due to his love for Him. This river too, flowing westward towards the temple, grows agitated in anticipation of seeing periya perumāḷ, and eastward, in sorrow at departing from Him. Thus, without distinction between chētana (Āḻvār) and achētana (river) entities, even those who walk near the temple experience this agitation.

Just as Nammāḻvār says in Thiruvāimoḻi 10.10.10 "adhaṉil periya eṉ avāvarach chūḻndhāy", periya perumāḷ envelops the Āḻvārs with His love. Likewise, Kāvēri envelops periya perumāḷ out of her love for Him. Parāśara Bhaṭṭar's Śrīraṅgarāja Stavam 1.21 eloquently describes Kāvēri's devotion: "dhugdhābdhir janakō jananīyahamiyam śrīrēva puthri vā śrīraṅgēśvara ēthadharhamiha kim kuryāmithvākulā | sañjaccāmara chandra chandana mahāmāṇikya mukthōthkarān kāvērī laharēekarairvidhadhathī paryēthi sā sēvyathām ||"

Just as it is challenging to navigate Kāvēri's floods, it is equally difficult to penetrate periya perumāḷ's resplendent radiance and admire His divine form. After entering Thiruvaraṅgam (Śrīraṅgam), even the brightness in Paramapadham diminished, like daylight. The radiance at Śrīraṅgam aids lowly saṃsārīs like night-time illumination. Emperumāṉ, amidst nityasūris, is like a sun among suns. But standing amidst saṃsārīs, who suffer from worldly sorrows, His radiance acquires dominance.

The Subālōpaniṣad 16 states: "māthā pithā bhrāthā nivāsaś śaraṇam suhruth gathir nārāyaṇa:" (Nārāyaṇa is mother, father, brother, dwelling place, means for attaining mōkṣa, friend, and the one attained in mōkṣa). The Āḻvār declares that for him, it is not Paramapadhanāthan, common to all; not Vyūha or Vibhava forms of perumāḷ, common to a few; not other Archāvatāra vigrahas common to other Āḻvārs; but only periya perumāḷ who is his father and mother. This exclusivity is emphasized by the term thāmē (He Himself). The Mahābhāratam Vana Parvam 192.56 ślōka reinforces this: "sarvēṣāmēva lōkānām pithā māthā cha mādhava: | gacchadhvamēnam śaraṇam śaraṇyam puruṣarṣabhā: ||" Unlike the cowherds, there is no need for difficult tasks like mountain-lifting to protect me. The Āḻvār pleads, "Is it not enough if You glance at me with Your comforting eyes?" Bestowing favors upon me. Even when emperumāṉ is not glancing at him, the Āḻvār acknowledges past favors, beseeching Him for this one. The Āḻvār yearns for emperumāṉ to say, "He has something good in him to be shown my mercy. He is my little fellow." The Āḻvār feels that only if emperumāṉ, the master, addresses him thus, confirming their master-servitor relationship, will his servitorship endure. This echoes incidents in the lives of pūrvāchāryas, such as Maṇakkāl Nambi addressing Thirumagizhmārban as "my son" and Piḷḷaippiḷḷai Āḻvāṉ referring to Appiḷḷai Āḻvāṉ as "little brother" and "my little fellow." The Āḻvār exclaims in deep anguish, "When I cry out to Him in sorrow, should He not rise? How can He sleep even after hearing my voice? Has His divine heart become so hardened?" The word amma indicates profound distress.

docs.text: Tamil Transliteration மேம்‌ பொருள்‌ போக விட்டு,மெய்ம்மையை மிக உணர்ந்து.ஆம்பரிசறிந்து கொண்டுஐம்‌ புலன்‌ அகத்தடக்கி.காம்பறத்‌ தலை சிரைத்தஉன்‌ கடைத்தலை இருந்து வாழும்‌.சோம்பரை உகத்தி போலும்‌,சூழ்‌ புனல்‌ அரங்கத்தானே ! mēm poruḻ pōga viṭṭumeymmaiyai miga uṇarnduāmbariśaṟindu koṇḍuaim pulan agattaḍakkikāmbaṟa ttalai śiraittuun kaḍaittalai irundu vāzumśōmbarai ugatti pōlumśūz punal araṅgattānē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh supreme Lord dwelling in the holy city of Srirangam made fertile by the surround- ing, flowing waters of Kāvēri! it seems You are pleased with those who refrain from leading prākṛtic (materialistic) way of life, and then, properly understand the nature of souls, and further, decide that the divine service done to You alone is the supreme end of one's life, and hence, who after restraining all their senses, withdraw themselves from all other pursuits and paths, and thus, who once for all, reject all unrighteous paths and stay at your threshold in order to do your divine service alone.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Alvār speaks about the nature of a true prapanna, a true bhāgavata. mēmpōrul refers to this body which can decay and is bound to perish once born. When a jīvātman realizes the essence of this life and understands that this body is perishable, while service to bhagavān is eternal, that jīvātman feels this body to be superficial. Only those who have surrendered to the lotus feet of Rañganātha can receive this beautiful knowledge; else, by māyā, the intertwined body makes the jīvātman feel "I am this dēha" which gives rise to ignorance. Refraining from such ignorance, a prapanna serves bhagavān. Until the jīvātman leaves material desire and the ignorance of "I am the body," he is destined to grow the tree called saṃsāra, as stated in Viṣṇu Purāṇa 7.11 as follows: "anāthmanyāthmā buddhir yā asve svam iti yā mati | saṃsāra-taru-sambhūti bījam ētat dvidhā sthitham ||" Hence, Alvār states to give up such traces completely. To give up such traces, the body must realize the divine nature of the ātman and īśvara. Once it realizes it is not the body, the tree called saṃsāra slowly withers away. When that ātman realizes its true nature, it realizes its svarūpam.

Even after realizing "I am not the body," the jīvātman must fully realize its true svarūpa—that it is the servant of bhagavān—and only then is liberation possible. When this knowledge is gifted to that jīvātman by bhagavān himself, it desires to serve the Lord eternally and strives to liberate itself from saṃsāra. In the attempt to liberate itself, it gives up the wealth, that is, the ignorance called "I am the body" and attaches itself to service to bhagavān. Realizing that removal of bondage through its own attempts is not possible, that jīvātman surrenders to bhagavān, keeping the Lord himself as the means to attain him. This is the essence of prapatti or śaraṇāgati, which was narrated to Arjuna by Kṛṣṇa in Bhagavad Gītā 18.66.

Alvār compares the means to attain bhagavān to hair. Just as hair brings a sense of prestige to a person, these means can bring the essence of pride—"I am my own protector" or "It is by my efforts that I am attaining bhagavān or achieving liberation". One must forget this thought and realize that it is not the means (Karma Yoga, Bhakthi Yoga and others) but the compassion of bhagavān which brings us closer to Him. He alone can get us out of saṃsāra; indeed, He is the means itself. This itself becomes a prosperity to the jīvātman.

Alvār goes to the extreme of saying "aimpulan agathtadakki"—that is, while a jīvātman performs kaiṅkarya (divine service) to bhagavān, it experiences happiness due to the divine nature of the service. But a true prapanna should renounce this happiness too. He must perform the service for the happiness of bhagavān and not for himself.

Looking at Thiruvāraṅga's face, Alvār states that He is smiling happily while observing such great devotees who have left everything and are performing their rituals and duties assigned by the śāstras for the happiness of bhagavān alone, because bhagavān has ordered them to do so. Such souls are the foremost among His devotees. Due to the disappearance of grey clouds called ignorance, the love and compassion of the Lord, known as dayā, eternally falls upon them like sunlight.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Tamil Transliteration அடிமையில்‌ குடிமை இல்லா,அயல்‌ சதுப்பேதி மாரில்‌,குடிமையில்‌ கடைமை பட்ட.குக்கரில்‌ பிறப்பர்‌ ஏலும்‌,முடியினில்‌ துளபம்‌ வைத்தாய்‌ !மொய்‌ கழற்கன்பு செய்யும்‌,அடியரை உகத்தி போலும்‌.அரங்க மா நகருளானே ! aḍimaiyil kuḍimai illāayal śaduppēdi mārilkuḍimaiyil kaḍaimai paṭṭakukkaril piṟappar ēlummuḍiyinil tuḻabam vaittāy !moy kazaṟkanbu śeyyumaḍiyarai ugatti pōlumaraṅga mā nagaruḻānē !

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord of the great city, Śrirangam! O supreme God with Tulasi leaves adorning your crown! it seems, You are more pleased with these who, though born in the lowest castes, seek the divine service under your pair of feet, and are highly devoted to You alone, than those who recite all the four Vedas, but do not seek the divine service under You, as the supreme goal.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Even those who do not recognize that performing kaiṅkaryam is inherent to their nature. It is fitting to think, "Kaiṅkaryam is natural to us. Just as we cannot live without food and water, we cannot exist without performing kaiṅkaryam." The Āḻvār refers to those who lack this understanding.

Those who differ from the chaturvēdhis who are not immersed in kaiṅkaryam. Sadhuppēdhimāril refers to those who study the four Vēdas. The benefit of Vēdic study is to realize that emperumāṉ is the master of all worlds, that we are His possessions, and that performing kaiṅkaryam to emperumāṉ and His devotees is our appropriate goal. Ayal signifies not knowing that the purpose of learning Vēdas is to obtain this knowledge. The Pādhmōttaram states: "viṣṇubhaktivihīnō yas sarvaśāstrārtha vēdhyapi | brāhmaṇyam tasya na bhavēt tasyōtpattir nirūpyatām ||" (Even if one knows the meanings of all śāstras, without devotion to Viṣṇu, one lacks the qualities of a brāhmaṇa, and their birth is questionable).

Kuḍimaiyil kaḍaimaippaṭṭa kukkaril piṟapparēlum - Those who, after many births of not following Vēdic injunctions and engaging in forbidden acts, are born into very low castes due to accumulated sins. Kukkar (kuṣka) refers to a class lower than chaṇḍāḷas. The Āḻvār's use of piṟapparēlum (even if they are born) indicates that birth status is not a determinant of understanding the meanings mentioned in the previous pāsuram. In Śrī Rāmāyaṇa Āraṇya Kāṇḍam 68.24, Śrī Rāma tells Lakṣmaṇa: "sarvatra khalu dṛśyante sādhavō dharmacāriṇa: | śūrā: śaraṇyās saumitrē tiryak yōni gatēṣvapi ||" (O Lakṣmaṇa! Those who are like sages, following the path of righteousness, fit to be surrendered to, are seen even among those born as animals and other species!). Just as emperumāṉ adorns tuḷasi on His head, these devotees are also fit to be kept on His head like tuḷasi. This adornment indicates His quality of being sarvēśvaran (lord of all).

These devotees cast aside their own happiness to serve only for His happiness, with affection, similar to sēvaḍi sevvi thirukkāppu (Thirupallāṇḍu 1). To them, this is the only purposeful way to spend time, and they consider this their goal. They consider His compassionate divine feet as the means. As mentioned in pāsuram 38 as sōmbar, they know that their ātma svarūpam (nature of the ātmā) is being eternally subservient to emperumāṉ and will not engage in self-protection. You delight in these followers who possess this knowledge, regardless of their lowly birth, rather than the chaturvēdhis who lack this understanding. The purpose of coming to Śrīraṅgam and reclining here is to hear these people who have affection towards You, even if they are of lowly birth. If You desired to hear only from the exalted, You would have remained in Śrīvaikuṇṭam.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord Ranganatha residing at Srirangam! O supreme Lord with God- dess Laksmi and the Śrivatsa mark adorning your broad chest! all the people on this earth should ever contemplate upon You and your consort, Goddess Sridevi, and then, they should install only both of You in their heart. If they do so, then even if they have committed the most heinous crimes, and so acquired such sins, they will not suffer from the fruits of those sins.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Hearken, gentle souls, to the wisdom of the Alvar, who once more doth proclaim the ineffable nature of the Divine Lord. He standeth beyond the confines of prakriti's elements, His essence a mystery that mortal minds can scarce comprehend. Verily, His virtues and qualities be infinite, stretching far beyond the reach of our humble understanding.

The Alvar, in his profound insight, declareth that only the Lord Himself knoweth the full measure of His divine play, His wondrous Leelas that unfold across the tapestry of creation. The sacred Taittiriya Upanishad, in its venerable verses, doth proclaim "aprāpya manasā saha" - even as the mind striveth to grasp His nature, it returneth baffled, unable to fathom the depths of His glory.

Yet, take heart, for though He be beyond the reach of common thought, He deigns to reside within the sanctum of pure hearts. As the hallowed Vishnu Sahasranama doth attest, He is "yōgihṛddhyānagamyaṃ" - accessible through the meditations of yogis whose minds are unburdened by impure thoughts. Thus, the Lord maketh His abode in the hearts of His true devotees. The Alvar, in his boundless wisdom, counseleth us to acknowledge our limitations. How can we, mere mortals, hope to sing the praises of He whom even Brahma and Rudra, mighty deities themselves, find beyond their capacity to laud? Nay, our mortal tongues and finite minds fall short in this endeavor.

Therefore, the Alvar guideth us toward a path most true and efficacious. Let us, in our devotion, turn to the chanting of His divine names and the constant remembrance of His glory. For in this sacred practice lies the key to accessing His divine presence. What sweeter pursuit can there be, what nobler endeavor, than to invoke the Supreme Lord through the utterance of His holy appellations?

Indeed, the Alvar assureth us, there existeth no higher or more potent means to draw near to the Divine than through the sincere and devoted chanting of His names. In this simple yet profound practice, we find the essence of bhakti, the purest form of devotion that bridgeth the gulf between the mortal and the Divine.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: If the devotees call You, as "Oh the supreme Lord dwelling in the Paramapada whom even the celestial beings cannot realise! O Lord with your head adorned by honey-laden garlands of Tulasi!" even if it be that they are of vile deeds, and they cause others commit crimes - nevertheless, if they could offer to us, the remnant of their food, it is, indeed, sacred and holy for us.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Verily, hearken to the words of the Alvar, who speaketh of the Lord who dwelleth eternally in Paramapadham, that celestial abode beyond the ken of even Brahma and the heavenly host. As those perched upon lofty balconies cannot discern the stars above, so too are the denizens of Satyaloka and other celestial realms unable to perceive the Lord of Paramapadham.

Though these celestial beings possess great knowledge and power, 'tis not sufficient to breach the gates of Paramapadham. The word "AgA" herein signifieth both impossibility and prohibition - as a lowly Chandala may not enter sacred grounds, so too are these celestial entities barred from Paramapadham's hallowed realm.

Yet, lo! The Alvars, those blessed souls, have glimpsed the Lord of Paramapadham. This cometh not from their own merit, but through His divine grace. As the Bhagavad Gita doth proclaim, those who fancy themselves as gods cannot perceive Him. The Alvars, like seafarers who cross vast oceans by ship, traverse the tumultuous sea of Samsara with Vishnu as their vessel. The celestial beings, in their pride, are as those who would attempt to swim across unaided.

The Alvars, in their wisdom, have surrendered fully to the Lord, recognizing Him as both the means and the end. They chant, "O Thou adorned with a honey dripping Tulasi garland upon Thy crown!" - proclaiming His supremacy among the gods and His sweetness that surpasseth all earthly delights.

Even those who once committed grievous sins - binding and slaughtering creatures for base sustenance - if they should come to know the Lord and take refuge in Him, they too may be redeemed. For the knowledge of the Divine transformeth the heart, turning even the most cruel to compassion. Alvar speaketh of the sanctifying power of the food remnants of the truly wise. As Parasara Bhattar once gifted his disciple Nanjiyer with such blessed morsels, so too can these remnants purify the partaker instantly, like a philosopher's stone transmuting base metal to gold. Thus doth the Alvar extol the greatness of the Lord and His devotees, showing that the path to salvation lieth not in celestial power, but in humble devotion and the grace of the Divine.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh the Lord of Śrirangam girt by seven Prakāras (ramparts)! I surmise that You have instructed the followers of Vedic lore as "O the reciters of the Vedas! O you who follow the age-old customs of your lineage faultlessly! even though the devotees of my feet have been born in the lowliest class (of the society), you have to bow to them; you offer to them whatever you know and whatever you can; you learn from them; treat them on par with me."

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Álvár calls upon the learned scholars, the Brāhmaṇas who have studied the four Vedas, to transcend the ego associated with being born into an upper caste and to eliminate the pride of possessing greater knowledge than others. He explains that discrimination based on appearance and birth is meaningless and should be abandoned, as such prejudices stem from the belief that materialistic goals are the ultimate pursuits. When the jīvātmā is eternal and born into this world through karma, assigned to a specific gender and clan, how could this matter to a mumukṣhu who has realized their true nature as śeṣa of Bhagavān? This is the essence of Álvár's teaching. Every jīvātmā has Bhagavān as the inner witness. Consequently, a prappanna will perceive Bhagavān everywhere. Why would such a person harm another simply due to their birth? A person with wealth, knowledge, or prestigious lineage may easily develop ego, as illustrated in the traditional saying: vidhyāmadho dhanamadhaḥ tṛtīyo'bhijano madhaḥ: ēthē madhāvaliptānām ētha ēva satām damaḥ. Therefore, Álvár advises against taking pride in one's language or acquired wisdom, recognizing that such knowledge is ultimately a gift from Bhagavān.

He further elaborates that speaking ill of others is unbecoming of a true Bhāgavata, and criticizing devotees of Bhagavān—particularly regarding their birth or background—is a grave transgression. Bhagavān himself teaches us to engage with his devotees: to share spiritual wisdom, show respect, and treat them as equivalent to the divine. Every devotee encountered should be honored as a manifestation of Bhagavān, for the divine resides within these devoted souls. Nammálvár's words in Thiruvāymoḻi 7.10 beautifully capture this sentiment: tīrththaṅgaḷē eṉṟu pūsiththu nalgiyuraippar tham dēviyarkē, even Nitya sūris speak about such great devotees! The teaching continues, niṉṉōdum okka vaḻipada aruḷiṉāy, suggesting that the devotees of Raṅganātha should be revered equally. These spiritual seekers must be respected as Ācāryas, regardless of their background or learning. Their sacred presence should be welcomed with utmost reverence and joy. This pasurama glorifies sripada teertham of Bhagavatas which have to taken with devotion and respect.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Oh Lord of the sacred temple city, Srirangam! among your devotees, if a section of devotees though born in higher classes of society, though taking a leading part in all activities, though well- versed in all holy scriptures, viz. the four Vedas and the six Vedāngas speak ill of other devotees belonging to lower classes of society, then, at that very moment, they are deemed to be.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Re-iterating the essence of the previous pasuram, Álvár speaks again to the learned ones that, though they might be well-read and versed in Vedas, if one speaks ill about the devotees of Bhagavān's devotees, they do not stand as learned ones; indeed, these are the lowest of all! The Vedas are considered to have six aṅgas: śikṣā (articulation or pronunciation of words), vyākaraṇa (grammar), chandhas (poetic metrics), niruktha (etymology), jyotiṣa (astrology), and kalpa. Parāśara Bhaṭṭar states in his Śrī Raṅgarāja Stavam that the Vedas with their aṅgas are speaking about none other than Śrī Raṅganātha! The ones who have studied these aṅgas and mastered them are worthy of celebration, as stated in the Purāṇas. This celebration arises from the nature of Vedas as apauruṣeya - not created by humans.

But Álvár provides an exception in celebrating such learned ones. If these learned ones end up speaking ill about a devotee, such people haven't learned the Vedas in their true sense. If a sense of hatred, especially towards the Bhāgavatas, arises even in those who have read the Vedas, how can they be considered learned? The Upaniṣads and Bhagavad Gītā, which are said to be the essence of the Vedas, state that devotees of īśvara are great and should be respected. Bhagavān goes to a greater extent, stating in Bhagavad Gītā 7.18: ātmaiva me matam āsthitaḥ sa hi yuktātmā mām evānuttamāṁ gatim - meaning the devotees who are ever devoted to Bhagavān and have considered him as the supreme goal, whose service to him is the supreme state, are very self of Bhagavān himself! Such jīvātmas are indeed rare. Hence, if Bhagavān has gone to such great lengths to praise his devotees and show the unbounded prema he has towards his dear devotees, how can the so-called learned ones speak ill of such great souls? Indeed, they haven't learned anything from the Vedas, which at their core speak about Bhagavān! Being a mumukṣhu is far from their sight when they do not have the maturity to look at the great devotees of Bhagavān.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: When Lord Siva with his matted locks of hair in which the girl makes a stroll (i.e. flows the holy river Gangā), and the four-faced Lord Brahmā are not able to perceive your true form - even though both of them (Siva and Brahmā) took to severe austerities (penance) for innumerable aeons and aeons and so both of them become dejected, Oh Lord Ranganatha! You have run swiftly towards the great devotee, Gajendra (the lordly elephant), and protected him by showering your grace on him. Oh Lord! are you without sympathy towards me? Why is it that I do not consider You as the only succour for me?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Bhagavān is the Creator of Jagat, the creator of Brahmā and Śiva. The Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad states: "eko ha vai nārāyaṇa āseet, na brahma, nēśāna" - meaning at the beginning, only Nārāyaṇa existed, neither Brahmā nor Īśa (Śiva) were present. Hence, without a second doubt, Nārāyaṇa is considered the Paramātma. The Vedas state this with multiple pramāṇas. At the same time, he is the final Puruṣārtha to attain Mokṣa, for all jīvātmas from Brahmā to animals. Poygai Álvár states similarly in Mudalai Thiruvandadi: "kadikkamalam thannuḷ irundhum kāṇkilān kaṇṇan adikkamalam thannai ayan" - even the lotus-born Brahmā, though born from Bhagavān's navel, is unable to see the lotus feet of Para Vasudeva (Kṛṣṇa).

The fact that Rudra provides a seat to Gaṅgā, which is the śrīpāda tīrtha of none other than Trivikrama avatāra of Bhagavān, speaks to the fact that even he is devoted to Nārāyaṇa. As the Taittirīya Upaniṣad states, "yatho vācho nivarthanthe" - words cannot describe Brahman. Brahmā performed the thiruvārdhana of Śrī Raṅganātha in Satya loka. Rudra performed penance near Chandrapuṣkaraṇi to remove the doṣa attained by removing Brahmā's 5th head. The same Śiva glorifies Śrīraṅgam and Raṅganātha while describing it to Nārada in Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. To access you and your divine form, even such great Sarva Jñānis have to perform severe austerities. How great is your compassion that you listened to the calls of Gajendra! The elephant finally understood its helplessness and called you with all love and devotion, surrendering to your lotus feet, praying to you as Ādimūla.

Indeed, as Bhagavān states in Bhagavad Gītā 11.48: "na veda-yajñādhyayanair na dānair na cha kriyābhir na tapobhir ugraiḥ evaṁ-rūpaḥ śhakya ahaṁ nṛi-loke draṣhṭuṁ tvad anyena kuru-pravīra" - neither by performing austerities nor by reading the Vedas can anyone see his divine form. But when questioned about what will give us his protection, especially from the tiger called Saṁsāra, Bhagavān assures in Bhagavad Gītā 18.66: "sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṁ śharaṇaṁ vraja ahaṁ tvāṁ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣhayiṣhyāmi mā śhuchaḥ" - the famous Charma śloka stating us to surrender to the divine feet of the Lord and perform all activities of Dharma for the sake of the Lord, abandoning its result. Bhagavān himself assures protection to these Prapannas. These are indeed the highest among all! Gajendra performing total surrender to Bhagavān at that moment, the Lord jumps from his seat to save his devotee without a moment's delay.

Álvár quotes two important points here: first, the surrendered ones need not fear anything when Sathya Saṅkalpa Mahā Viṣṇu has assured their protection. Secondly, when Bhagavān himself accepts the devotion of devatas as well as an elephant equally, and even aided the elephant much faster, it states that there is no sense in discriminating people. Any jīvātma which desires Bhagavān alone is worthy to be celebrated.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: The devotee Toṇḍaraḍippoḍi Āḻvār (the dust of the feet of the devotees of the Lord) who is ever at the service of offering Tulasi garlands, has sung in praise of the Lord Visņu (Śri Ranganatha) of Śrirangam, Lord Kṛṣṇa Himself who has slain the large elephant in ruts at the gate of the great city, Mathurai decked with palatial pure white marble buildings. This poet-devotee hopes that even if his small poetic composition lacks in grandeur, it would be accepted by the great Lord as sweet and sacred.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Completing the divine Tirumalai, Álvār surrenders this set of 45 poems to Bhagavān's lotus feet. Thoṇḍaraḍippoḍi sol – in line with his service orientation towards bhāgavathas, he has Thoṇḍaraḍippoḍi as his name. It is clear from this that his identity is not jñānam, ānandham, or bhagavat śeṣatvam [our sacred texts say that ātmā is full of jñānam (knowledge), ānandham (happiness), and is śeṣabhūthan (carrying service to Emperumān)], but bhāgavatha śeṣatvam (service to followers of Emperumān). Just as Nammālvār in his Thiruvāimozhi 7.1.11 said "thoṇḍar thoṇḍar thoṇḍar thoṇḍan Śatakōpan" (Śatakōpan, another name of Nammālvār, is Emperumān's follower's follower's follower's follower), this Álvār called himself Thoṇḍaraḍippoḍi (the dust sticking to the feet of a follower of Emperumān). By following naichyānusandhānam, Álvār states these poems to be lowly (but in reality are gold of bhakti extracted from Vedānta).

Álvār sees Namperumal smile at him with happiness, which makes him exclaim that his gibberish words have pleased Bhagavān, who defeated the elephant in his Kṛṣṇa avatāra, just as a child's words please the father.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: He has shown him that the insentient things seen around are fleeting like lightning. He has revealed the four Vedas and is like the light of a lamp, dispelling the darkness called ignorance from him. He has given him knowledge, clear like the blemishless moon risen on the horizon, and as perceptible as the moon shining in the sky above. He has shown him that the ātmā is distinct and free from the disease, old age, and rebirth associated with the insentient things seen around. He does not deign to grant him Kaivalya. He has shown him His precious form, which cannot be cognized by anyone at any time. He possesses a human form composed of the divine elements (Śuddha Sattva). He is pleasant and refreshing to devotees like cool water, and to inimical beings, like fire. He is the effulgence within all and is supremely radiant. The sacred feet of such a One are enshrined in his heart.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār expresses his gratitude to Bhagavān in this pāsuram. Tirunēṭuntāṇṭakam was composed by Āḻvār during the final stage of his life. Throughout his life, he had repeatedly pleaded with Bhagavān to grant him the vision of His Divya Maṅgala Rūpa. Indeed, the biography of Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār records that Bhagavān, accompanied by His divine consort, appeared before him in the form of a newly married couple and personally initiated him into the sacred Aṣṭākṣarī mantra. From that moment onward, Āḻvār became fully immersed in bhakti. Therefore, he reflects here on how Bhagavān blessed him and redirected his mind towards the Lord's lotus feet. Bhagavān revealed to Āḻvār the transient nature of this material world and the eternal nature of the ātmā, which is free from disease, suffering, and decay. This knowledge was bestowed upon him with the sudden brilliance and clarity of a lightning flash.

Similar to the opening pāsuram of Tiruvāymoḻi by Nammāḻvār, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār also acknowledges that Bhagavān alone grants the knowledge that dispels the darkness of ignorance. What made Āḻvār even more grateful was that, in addition to imparting divine knowledge, the Lord also revealed His own divine form, which is not constituted of the elements of this material world. Unlike material substances, His Divya Maṅgala Rūpa is completely free from rajas and tamas and is therefore described as Śuddha Sattva. Just as the material world is constituted of five prākṛtika elements, the Lord's divine form is said to be constituted of five Śuddha Sattva principles, glorified in the Pañcopaniṣad mantras as Parameṣṭhi, Pumān, Nivṛtta, Viśva, and Sarva. Āḻvār is overwhelmed with gratitude that the Lord revealed such a transcendent form, a vision inaccessible even to Brahmā and Rudra. It is through the Lord's grace in bestowing both this divine knowledge and the experience of His divine form that Āḻvār was able to develop profound love and devotion towards Him.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: He stands in a divine form as the Trinity. Yet, when the celestials conceive of their forms differently, one (Brahmā's) is of the nature of gold, one (Śiva's) is of the nature of red-hot fire, and one (the Lord's) is of the nature of the great ocean. Upon examining these three forms along with their associated natures, it is seen that our Master is the One who created the Pañcabhūtas, namely Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether (primary creation), and who stands pervading the innumerable and distinct orderly creations (secondary creation), which shine forth as a unified effulgence of love, bearing the nature of the clouds.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār beautifully expounds the supremacy of Bhagavān (Paratattvam) in this passage. He first declares, "He stands in a divine form as the Trinity" (pār uruvil nīr eri kāl viśumbum āgi). Through this, Āḻvār conveys that Bhagavān Himself created Brahmā and Rudra and entered into them as their Antaryāmī to carry out the functions of creation and destruction respectively. Thus, the three fundamental activities of the universe—creation, preservation, and destruction—are ultimately performed by Bhagavān alone.

At first glance, it may appear that Āḻvār is equating all three members of the Trinity. However, he clarifies this in the following line. While Bhagavān enters Brahmā and Rudra as their Antaryāmī and empowers them to perform their respective functions, He also distinctly manifests as Viṣṇu. In this way, Āḻvār establishes both the Lord's indwelling presence within all beings and His unique, independent identity. Although these three forms appear different, Āḻvār speaks of Brahmā and Rudra in terms of their indwelling Self, namely Bhagavān Himself. Therefore, the One who truly possesses and governs all these forms is none other than our beloved Master.

He is the One who first brought forth the pañcabhūtas and subsequently carried out the secondary creation of all animate and inanimate entities. Yet His role does not end with creation alone. Having brought all beings into existence, He enters each of them as Antaryāmī, sustaining them from within and enabling all their activities. As their inner ruler and support, He continually provides the very life force and existence upon which they depend.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: It is said that the cloud-hued Lord, together with the effulgence of Lakṣmī, shone with a white body in a gigantic form as the Tortoise at the time when the nectar was obtained from the Milk Ocean (in Kṛta Yuga), and that He was of a red hue in Tretā Yuga. The great Lord of blue complexion (in Kali Yuga) cannot be conceived of as possessing any single form, nature, or color. Apart from praising Him continuously, age after age, through mere imagination, has anyone truly seen the dark-bodied, red-eyed Lord as he has seen Him?

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
In the first pāsuram, the Lord revealed to Āḻvār the futility of attachment to the body and the individual self, as well as the inadequacy of remaining in kaivalya. He also granted him the vision of His own incomparable beauty. In the second pāsuram, He revealed that He alone, and none other, is the sole Master of all. Having received these revelations, Āḻvār now stands like a chaste wife wholly dedicated to her husband. In this pāsuram, Āḻvār declares that he beholds the Lord in His true nature and in the full splendour of His divine form, unlike others who, throughout the ages, perceive Him only according to the limitations imposed by their surroundings and mental dispositions, shaped as they are by the three guṇas of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

During Kṛta Yuga, sattva predominates, and therefore people perceive the Lord as white, the colour traditionally associated with sattva. In Tretā Yuga, rajas becomes dominant, and the Lord is seen in red, the colour corresponding to that quality. In Dvāpara Yuga, where rajas and tamas exist in a mixed proportion, the perceived colour is understood to be intermediate in nature. In Kali Yuga, tamas predominates, and its associated colour is black. Yet, since people of this age are generally not inclined towards God and are unable to perceive Him as He truly is, the Lord remains in His natural hue, the deep blue complexion of Nilamegha Śyāma, manifesting in His own intrinsic splendour.

Āḻvār also beautifully extols the divinity of Mahālakṣmī through the phrase kaḍalamutam koṇḍa kālam. When the Milk Ocean was churned, not only did the devas obtain nectar, but the Lord Himself gained the supreme nectar in the form of Mahālakṣmī, who emerged from those sacred waters. Āḻvār, in turn, partakes of that same nectar through his loving glorification of the Lord and His divine consort. Thus, the episode becomes not merely an account of cosmic events, but a celebration of the inseparable union of the Divine Couple and the bliss experienced by the devotee who contemplates them.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Obedient mind! We can live worthily in the company of the Nityasūris if we can forever, without interruption, eulogize through the Tirumantra that Protector (mantrāṁ trāyate iti mantraḥ, “the one who protects the chanter”), who is the originator of Indra and Brahmā (in secondary creation); who caused the five elements, namely Earth, Wind, Fire, Water, and Ether (in primary creation); who is accurately revealed in the Tamil Prabandham and the Sanskrit scriptures; who is the inner controller of everything in the four directions; who ordains the Moon and the Sun; who is the Immaculate One who, though dwelling in their hearts, cannot be understood even by the gods; and who is glorified in the Upaniṣads, the concluding portion of the sages' scriptures.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
This pāsuram glorifies the Tirumantram, the sacred Aṣṭākṣarī mantra. Similar to the teachings found in Tiruvāymoḻi, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār instructs the mind to contemplate the Supreme Lord through the recitation and meditation of the Tirumantram. The Nārāyaṇopaniṣad says the following about the Aṣṭākṣarī mantra:

om namo nārāyaṇāyēti ma̍ntrōpā̠sakaḥvaikuṇṭhabhuvanalōka̍-ṅgami̠ṣyati ।

This states that one who performs upāsanā on this sacred mantra ultimately attains Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Abode from which the jīvātmā never returns to the cycle of worldly existence. Āḻvār echoes the same truth in this pāsuram when he urges, "O mind, recite the Tirumantram so that we may dwell in the company of the Nityasūris, the eternal servants of the Lord in Vaikuṇṭha."

Addressing his own mind, and thereby instructing all devotees, Āḻvār asks it to meditate upon Bhagavān, the source of even Brahmā and Rudra. This teaching is once again affirmed in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad as follows:

nā̠rā̠ya̠ṇādbra̍hmā jā̠yatē ।nā̠rā̠ya̠ṇādru̍drō jā̠yatē।

This declares that Brahmā and Rudra emerged from Nārāyaṇa. The pāsuram thus serves as a clear demonstration of how the Divya Prabandham embodies the very essence of Vedānta. This same Nārāyaṇa is the creator of the five great elements, the Pañcabhūtas, which constitute the material universe. Āḻvār further proclaims that this Supreme Lord is glorified both by the Vedas, the repository of Sanskrit revelation, and by the Prabandha Mālai, the treasure of Tamil revelation.

Āḻvār also affirms that the Moon, the Sun, and all the directions function entirely under the Lord's sovereignty. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad states the same truth:

hī̠ṣā-'smā̠dvāta̍ḥ pavatē । bhī̠ṣōdē̍ti̠ sūrya̍ḥ । bhīṣā-'smādagni̍śchēndra̠ścha । mṛtyurdhāvati pañcha̍ma iti ।

This means that the wind blows, the sun shines, Agni and Indra perform their respective functions, and even Death itself carries out its duty out of reverential awe for Brahman. That same Brahman remains beyond the comprehension of even the devas. He cannot be fully grasped by the mind or expressed through ordinary thought, a truth echoed in the Upaniṣadic statement aprāpya manasā saha. Thus, the theological vision presented in this pāsuram closely mirrors the teachings of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad. Through his divine insight, Āḻvār exhorts all seekers to receive the Tirumantram through proper initiation from an Ācārya, constantly remember the Lord through its recitation, attain His eternal abode, and abide forever in unending bliss.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: One leg stopped short of sweeping the Earth and the waters with a single charming step. The other leg, beyond the imagination of the fortunate Mahābali, who beheld the Lord face to face, rose up from the sacrificial ground and penetrated the cosmic egg, reaching up to Brahmaloka beyond the vast heavens, the cool Moon, the Sun, and even the world of stars. He prostrates before the sacred feet, fresh as newly blossomed flowers, of his Father, who stood thus and took possession of all the worlds.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār visualizes the Vāmana and Trivikrama incarnations in this pāsuram. Here, the relationship between the jīvātmā and Īśvara, namely that of servant and Master, is beautifully brought out. When Mahābali agreed to grant the dwarf brāhmaṇa a piece of land measuring three footsteps, the Lord revealed His true majesty and resolved to measure the entire universe with just two steps, thereby once again establishing His sovereignty over all creation.

With His first step, He encompassed the Earth, the waters, and all the worlds below. His second step expanded beyond all measure, reaching the very limits of the universe. At the boundary of Satyaloka, Brahmā worshipped those divine lotus feet with great reverence. It is said that Dharma Devī herself flowed as sacred water upon those feet, and from that divine contact the holy river Gaṅgā came into existence. Thus, those lotus feet became the source of one of the most sacred rivers revered throughout the worlds.

Āḻvār therefore offers his prostrations to those very feet that rose beyond the Moon, the Sun, and even Satyaloka; to those feet that bestowed eternal blessings upon Mahābali; and to those feet from which the sacred Gaṅgā emerged. The Lord's cosmic stride was not merely an act of measuring the worlds, but a revelation of His supreme lordship and boundless grace.

Through this contemplation, Āḻvār recalls that the same Trivikrama is the Supreme Īśvara, the ruler and owner of all existence. In contrast, all jīvātmās are eternally dependent upon Him and exist solely as His servants. By meditating upon the Trivikrama incarnation, Āḻvār reaffirms this fundamental truth of existence: that Bhagavān is the eternal Master, and the essential nature (svarūpa) of the jīvātmā is loving and eternal service to Him.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: The Lord of the Nityasūris, the unique Rider of Garuḍa of lovely wings, who, by nature, has hands far-flung and generous to satiety (towards His devotees), does not grace, out of anger, the rākṣasas (inimical people). Mind! Let us prostrate, eulogizing His feet through all towns relished by Him on the way, lovely Kōvalūr surrounded by tanks and with spread-out fields growing precious crops, where pearl-like droplets in mire oozing out from tall bamboo trees, brought and thrown about in the fields by the overflowing water of river Pennai are discarded (by the farmers).

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Having given a magnificent description of the Lord in His Trivikrama avatāra in the previous pāsuram, Āḻvār need not lament that he was not present during that divine age to behold the Lord with his own eyes. The same Lord continues to reside at Tirukkōvaḷūr in the very form in which He manifested during that avatāra, making Himself available to devotees born in later generations. Thus, the blessings of witnessing Trivikrama are not confined to those who lived during the avatāra itself, but remain accessible to all who approach Him with devotion.

Āḻvār's mention of the Nityasūris and Garuḍa highlights the transcendental nature of Nārāyaṇa. In Paramapada, the Lord has already bestowed the highest gift upon the Nityasūris, namely Himself, and there are no hostile or inimical beings there from whom protection is required. Therefore, references to the Nityasūris and Garuḍa serve to emphasize the Lord's divine majesty while simultaneously drawing attention to His extraordinary accessibility through His avatāras and arcā manifestations in this world.

The Lord who transcends all realms willingly descends among humanity so that ordinary beings may approach Him, worship Him, and experience His grace. Reflecting upon this boundless accessibility, Āḻvār turns to his own mind and urges it to undertake a sacred pilgrimage through the Lord's temple towns. Just as a weary traveller carefully chooses hospitable resting places while avoiding barren and inhospitable regions, the devotee should seek refuge in the Divya Deśams where the Lord graciously resides. Journeying from one sacred abode to another, singing His glories along the way, the mind becomes steadily absorbed in divine contemplation and progresses towards its ultimate goal of eternal service to the Lord.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Mind! Let us go to worship lovely Kōvalūr, guarded by the chaste virgin (Durgā) residing in the Vindhyas, with fragrant tanks, broad streets and lotus ponds, where the chieftains of the hills do service, the town of the Lord who wielded the lovely axe (as Paraśurāma) annihilating the Chieftains (like Kārtavīryārjuna), and the Lord (as Kṛṣṇa) who defeated the army led by Subrahmaṇya who wielded the unique spear in the huge sea containing the mountains.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Because of his intense devotion, Āḻvār becomes concerned for the safety of the Lord, who stands before the world in all the beauty, tenderness, and charm of youthful splendour, as described in the previous pāsurams, amidst people of asuric disposition. Such is the nature of divine love that the devotee, forgetting the Lord's omnipotence, becomes anxious for His well-being and protection.

A similar sentiment is seen in the Rāmāyaṇa. When Vibhīṣaṇa approached Rāma on the seashore seeking refuge, Sugrīva strongly opposed accepting him. Since Vibhīṣaṇa had come from the hostile environment of Laṅkā, Sugrīva feared that he might intend harm to Rāma. In response, Rāma reassured him by explaining His unwavering vow to protect anyone who sought refuge in Him, His code of righteousness, and His incomparable prowess. In the same manner, Āḻvār is now made to realize the Lord's supreme ability to overcome all opposing forces, and this realization fills him with joy and reassurance.

The pāsuram alludes to two well-known episodes from the Purāṇas. According to the ancient legend, all mountains once possessed wings and moved freely through the skies. Their constant movement caused great disturbance to the worlds, prompting Indra to sever their wings. Only the mountain Maināka escaped this fate by concealing itself beneath the ocean. Later, Subrahmaṇya, also known as Skanda, the commander-in-chief of the celestial armies, discovered Maināka and cut off its wings with his spear.

Āḻvār then recalls an even greater demonstration of the Lord's supremacy. The same Skanda, together with his father Śiva, came to the aid of Bāṇāsura when Kṛṣṇa waged war against him. Despite the combined strength of these mighty allies, they were effortlessly subdued by Kṛṣṇa. Through this remembrance, Āḻvār understands that the Lord who conquered such formidable opponents has nothing to fear from any hostile force. The pāsuram therefore transforms the devotee's anxiety into delight, as Āḻvār reflects upon the Lord's boundless power, which remains ever ready to protect both Himself and His devotees.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Lord Nīrakam (of the nature of water)! Lord at the top on the lofty mountain (Tirumalai)! Lord pleasing like (full) moon shining in a small place (Nilaṭiṭiṅgal Tuṇḍan)! Lord Uraga in Kāñcī! Lord reposing at Vēṅka near the lovely stream (Lord Yathōktakāri)! Lord in the hearts of those who meditate on you! Lord at Kāraga eulogized by the world! Lord like water-laden cloud (at Karvāṇam)! Deceitful Lord! Lord at Tiruppērai on the southern side of the highly cherished and lovely Kāvēri river! Lord established in my mind without parting ever! The lofty Lord! I have adorned your sacred feet.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
Āḻvār was unable to physically experience the divine beauty and glorious qualities of the Lord that he had envisioned in the preceding pāsurams. As this composition belongs to the final period of his life, he would have been advanced in age and no longer possessed the strength required to undertake such a journey. Realizing his own limitations, he turns directly to the Lord, knowing that Bhagavān is not only the ultimate goal (upeya) but also the means (upāya) to attain that goal.

With this understanding, Āḻvār appeals to the Lord through the sentiment expressed in kūvuḍal varuḍal ceyyāy—"Either call me to You or come to me Yourself." This is an appeal founded entirely upon divine grace (Tiruvaruḷ). The devotee recognizes that his own efforts are insufficient and therefore seeks the Lord's intervention, whether by drawing him into His presence or by personally granting him the desired vision.

One may wonder why Āḻvār addresses the Lord in various sacred abodes when his longing is specifically to behold Him at Tirukkōvaḷūr. The answer lies in the Lord's all-pervading presence and His equal manifestation in every Divya Deśam. Just as the Sun illuminates the entire world uniformly while remaining one and the same, the Lord graciously resides in all the places that He has chosen as His abodes. Though the forms may appear in different locations, the Lord who dwells within them is one and indivisible.

Therefore, Āḻvār understands that his plea will reach the Lord regardless of the particular shrine to which it is addressed. Whether he prays at Tirukkōvaḷūr or at any other sacred abode, the same compassionate Lord hears his appeal. This conviction deepens his dependence upon divine grace, for he knows that the Lord who resides everywhere is fully capable of responding to the yearning of His devotee and granting the longed-for union.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: Lord at Māmallaipuram where precious gems are brought by ships and dumped! Lord of the town of Kāñcī with fortifications! Lord at Tiruppērai! Lord who has Śiva with Pārvatī beside him on the left and decorated by garland of fragrant honey-soaked bilva flowers on his chest, at His side! Lord of the Milk-ocean! Lord who came on the earth (in avatāras)! Lord at the top of the cool mountain (Tirumalai)! Lord Pavaḷavanna (at Kāñcī)! Looking for you all over, this fickle-minded self is wallowing in this body.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
In an earlier pāsuram, Āḻvār celebrated the boundless compassion of the Lord, who extends His grace even to those who are not inclined towards Him. If such is the Lord's nature, Āḻvār wonders why He has neither summoned him to Tirukkāñūr nor come personally to grant him His presence. The only explanation he can find is the burden of his own accumulated sins, which continue to obstruct the fulfilment of his longing.

Filled with this sense of helplessness, Āḻvār laments his condition. He finds himself unable either to endure the separation from the Lord or to cast aside the body that sustains that suffering. Thus, he remains caught in a state of anguish, yearning for union with the Lord while feeling constrained by the limitations imposed by karma.

The phrase "Vaṅkaṭṭāl māmaṇi vandu uṇḍu" is explained through a beautiful analogy. Precious gems are often brought by ships from the depths of the ocean and deposited upon the shore. In the same way, the Lord, who eternally resides in Paramapada, has graciously descended and established Himself on the seashore at Māmallapuram for the delight and benefit of His devotees. Just as a rare jewel becomes accessible when brought from distant waters to the shore, the Lord has made Himself easily accessible to those who seek Him.

Through this imagery, Āḻvār highlights the Lord's extraordinary simplicity and accessibility. Though He is the Supreme Being who transcends all worlds, He willingly leaves His exalted abode and manifests among devotees so that they may approach Him without difficulty. Yet, despite such accessibility, Āḻvār feels unable to attain Him and therefore attributes the delay solely to his own shortcomings. This pāsuram thus becomes a moving expression of humility, longing, and the pain of separation experienced by a devotee who sees the Lord's nearness everywhere but feels himself unworthy of receiving His grace.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: You are in the south (at Tirumalirumcōlai) eulogized by the worlds. You are in the north (at Tirumalai). You are in the west (at Śrīraṅgam). You are in the east (at Kaṇṇapuram) like an elephant in rut. You are always in the forefront of the Nityasūris. You are at Tirumōlikkalam with effulgence for veneration by subsequent generations of devotees. You are the primordial Lord. My cherished Lord! Lord with the glory of protecting the seven worlds! What does this insignificant devotee, bereft of any means, know apart from saying "My Elephant! My Elephant!"

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
In the fourth pāsuram, Āḻvār had declared, "Mantirattai mantirattai maṟavādu eṉṟum vāḻttiyēl vāḻalām"—that one can truly thrive by constantly glorifying the Protector through the Tirumantram without interruption. Reflecting upon this, Āḻvār wonders whether the Lord had refrained from appearing before him because He might have mistaken this constant recitation for an act of personal sādhanā undertaken to attain Him. However, Āḻvār clarifies that this was never his intention. His purpose was merely to remind himself of the true nature of the soul, to remain absorbed in thoughts of the Lord, and to spend his time in a meaningful and beneficial manner while awaiting divine grace.

In this pāsuram, Āḻvār expresses both his own utter helplessness and the Lord's incomparable greatness. He emphasizes that attainment of the Lord is not the result of individual effort but solely of the Lord's compassion and initiative. To illustrate this truth, Āḻvār compares the Lord to a majestic elephant.

An elephant cannot be ignored because of its immense size and commanding presence. Yet, despite its strength, it can be controlled only when it willingly cooperates. A rider cannot mount an elephant through his own effort alone; the elephant itself must kneel down and make it possible. Likewise, if it so chooses, the elephant can lift a person with its trunk and place him upon its back. Through this analogy, Āḻvār conveys that the jīvātmā cannot attain Bhagavān merely through personal endeavour. The Lord Himself must graciously make Himself accessible and elevate the devotee through His own will.

Āḻvār further compares the Lord to the mighty Diggajas, the celestial elephants that are traditionally said to uphold and protect the directions of the universe. In a similar manner, the Lord stands protecting and sustaining the world through His presence in the great sacred abodes of Vēṅkaṭam, Kāṇṇapuram, Tirumalirumcōlai, and Śrīraṅgam. From these holy places, He extends His grace to all who seek Him.

Thus, although the Lord is immeasurably exalted, He remains within easy reach of His devotees. By contemplating His presence in these sacred kṣetras, Āḻvār finds solace in the assurance that the Lord who sustains the universe is also the compassionate Master who graciously makes Himself accessible to those who depend entirely upon Him.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: She wears choice silk sari (to attract Him). She feels faint and sobs. She has no desire for the dolls. With her cool and drawn-out eyes filled with tears, she does not lie down. She does not stay on my lap even for a moment. She murmurs, "Where is my Lord of Tiruvāraṅgam?" When I asked the (female) soothsayer, "Tell me truly who did this to my young doe with locks of hair humming with lovely bees spitting the honey sucked by them?", she said, "The Lord of sea-hue did this. My life-companions! Who else is there to protect her (if He does not)!"

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The ten pāsurams beginning with this one are spoken through the voice of the mother of a heroine who suffers the anguish of separation from her beloved after having experienced union with him. At this stage, Āḻvār has attained complete spiritual maturity. His mind is fixed exclusively upon the Lord and upon nothing else, embodying the principle of Ananyā Śeṣatva, the state of belonging solely to Bhagavān. This exclusive devotion is traditionally expressed through the mood of a chaste heroine whose thoughts are entirely absorbed in her beloved.

When femininity is attributed to Āḻvār in such passages, it does not refer in any way to physical characteristics. Rather, it signifies a particular spiritual disposition and emotional attitude towards the Lord. The soul, recognizing its complete dependence upon Bhagavān, assumes the role of the heroine, while the Lord is understood as the sole beloved and protector. Such imagery serves as a powerful means of expressing the intensity of divine love experienced by the devotee.

The love experienced by Āḻvār has now become so overwhelming that it leaves no room for self-control or ordinary worldly awareness. Because of the depth of this experience, the condition of Āḻvār is portrayed through the observations of a mature and concerned mother. This literary device allows the inner state of the devotee to be described from an external perspective while preserving the emotional richness of the experience.

In this pāsuram, the mother describes the condition of her daughter, the heroine, whose suffering has become evident to all around her. Seeking to discover the cause of this mysterious affliction, she approaches a godly inclined soothsayer and asks for an explanation. Upon learning that the heroine's condition arises not from any worldly cause but from her intense love for Bhagavān, the mother turns to the maidens gathered around her and reflects upon the situation.

She realizes that the Lord alone is the true protector and refuge of all souls. If the very One who exists to safeguard His devotees does not come to the aid of this love-stricken heroine, then who else could possibly offer her protection? Thus, the pāsuram becomes a poignant expression of absolute dependence upon Bhagavān, emphasizing that the soul has no refuge apart from Him and that relief from the anguish of separation can come only through His grace.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: With her heart melting and eyes shedding tears, she stands languished. She sighs deeply. She has not known food or sleep. She says, "The perfectly lovely Lord sleeping on the poison-emitting Ādiśeṣa!" She says, "The youthful Lord at Tiruvāli with fields full of lovely fragrant flowers!" Again, bringing to mind the flying banner with Garuḍa of lovely feathers, she says, "Friends, shall we go to lovely Tiruvāraṅgam?" O! My sins! Having got a girl who is not under my control, I got censured by the people of this sprawling world.

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
In the previous pāsuram, the heroine had become so overwhelmed by her love for the Lord that she lost awareness of herself and her surroundings. However, when the soothsayer uttered the words "the sea-hued Lord," she regained a measure of consciousness and immediately burst into lamentation, as described in this pāsuram. The mention of the Lord was enough to awaken her from her state of inward absorption and intensify the pain of separation that already consumed her heart.

When the matronly woman complains that she stands censured by the people, she is not criticizing the heroine's conduct. Rather, she laments her own inability to find a remedy for the heroine's condition. Observers naturally expect a mother to comfort and restore her daughter, but finding herself powerless before an affliction born of divine love, she becomes the object of criticism and concern. Her grief arises not from embarrassment, but from helplessness.

This pāsuram explores more deeply the experience of viraha, the anguish of separation in devotional love. The heroine's suffering symbolizes the longing of the individual soul for union with Bhagavān. Having once tasted the sweetness of His presence, the soul finds separation unbearable and becomes incapable of taking delight in anything else. The intensity of this longing is presented not as a weakness, but as the natural consequence of profound devotion.

The reference to the "sea-hued Lord" evokes the image of Lord Viṣṇu, whose divine complexion is traditionally compared to the deep blue of the ocean. The very mention of this description stirs the heroine's heart, illustrating how even the slightest reminder of the Lord can awaken powerful emotions in a true devotee. For one whose mind is wholly absorbed in Bhagavān, a single word, image, or memory is sufficient to rekindle both joy and sorrow.

The pāsuram also beautifully illustrates mādhurya bhāva, the devotional mood in which the soul relates to the Lord as a beloved. In this mode of devotion, the intensity, exclusiveness, and purity associated with human love are employed to express the soul's longing for the Divine. Through the voice of the heroine, Āḻvār conveys the depth of his own devotion, portraying a love so complete that separation from the Lord becomes the soul's greatest suffering and remembrance of Him its only solace.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: With tear drops trickling down her twin breasts, and feeling weary, she asks her parrot to repeat by prompting it, such as, "Lord who protected from hailstorm by lifting the hill!" "Lord Uraga at lovely and highly desired Kāñcī!" "Lord who embraced the tender arms (of Sītā) by breaking the bow!" "The Master who is reposing in Vēṅka!" "The Lord who vanquished the wrestlers at one time and made them powerless!" and, "My youthful Lord with palms that split open (the mouth) of the horse Keśī."

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
The mother observed that the repeated chanting of the Lord's names had a soothing effect on the heroine's distressed condition. Hoping to bring her further comfort, she brought the heroine's pet parrot and placed it beside her, expecting it to repeat the divine names as it had been taught. However, the parrot remained silent. Traditional commentators explain this silence through the analogy of a disciple who, even after receiving instruction from an Ācārya, does not display his learning independently in the presence of the teacher. Out of humility and reverence, the disciple speaks only when prompted.

Accordingly, the parrot waited in silence until the heroine herself addressed it. Once encouraged by its mistress, it began to repeat the sacred names of the Lord, thereby offering comfort to the very one who had taught it. The scene beautifully illustrates the reciprocal nature of devotion, where even a simple creature becomes an instrument of divine remembrance and consolation.

A distinctive feature of Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār's devotional experience is his profound fulfillment in the Arcāvatāra. While the other Āḻvārs frequently celebrate the Lord's transcendence in Paramapada, His accessibility through various avatāras, and His presence in Arcā forms, Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār displays a particularly intense attachment to the Arcā manifestations found in the Divya Deśams. For him, the Lord enshrined in the temple is not different from the Lord who appeared in the great avatāras described in the scriptures.

In this pāsuram, Āḻvār emphasizes the essential oneness of the Lord in both Arcā and Avatāra. While standing before the Arcā form, he recalls the deeds performed during Kṛṣṇa's earthly incarnation and addresses the Lord directly as the very same Kṛṣṇa who protected His devotees. Thus, there is no distinction between the deity worshipped in the temple and the Lord who enacted divine sports in ages past.

Āḻvār specifically recalls the Govardhana episode through the words, "You warded off the hailstones by lifting a stone aloft." Here, Govardhana Hill is deliberately referred to as merely a stone in order to highlight the effortless nature of Kṛṣṇa's act. What appears to the world as a mighty mountain is, from the perspective of the omnipotent Lord, no more difficult to lift than a small stone.

The episode also reveals the wondrous and inscrutable ways of Bhagavān. When torrential rains and hailstones threatened the inhabitants of Gokula, the Lord chose to protect them by using another stone, Govardhana itself, as their shelter. In this sense, He countered stone with stone, much as one might speak of fighting fire with fire. Through this delightful recollection, Āḻvār celebrates both the Lord's infinite power and His affectionate concern for those who seek refuge in Him.

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text: After listening to the sonorous names of the Lord of Śrī at Tiruttaṅkal and Tiruvēṅka, effulgent like the rising Sun, the cloud-hued Lord at Kuruṅkuḍi, who is supreme and beyond the three types of souls (baddha, mukta and nitya) in the three worlds, the insatiable Nectar beyond scrutiny, the immaculate Lord at Śrīraṅgam, the Lord in the hearts of pure souls, the Lord who dispels ignorance like the darkness from the light of the lamp and who is pleasingly lustrous like emerald, by the obedient parrot, she folded her hands and prostrated, saying "Welcome; I am profited by bringing you up."

docs.title: Purport
docs.text:
As explained in the previous pāsuram, the parrot began reciting the names of the Lord after being prompted by the heroine. Hearing those sacred names emerge from the bird she had lovingly nurtured and instructed, the heroine experiences immense joy. She feels that her efforts in raising and teaching the parrot have finally borne fruit, for it has now become an instrument for glorifying Bhagavān.

The phrase "kaikkūppi vaṇaṅgināḷē" indicates that the heroine folded her hands in reverence and saluted the parrot. At first glance, this may appear surprising. Why should the heroine offer such respect to a mere parrot, especially one that may be regarded as her own disciple? The commentators explain that the significance lies not in the bird itself, but in what it is doing. By reciting the divine names of the Lord, the parrot assumes the role of a Bhāgavata, one who glorifies Bhagavān, and thereby becomes worthy of veneration.

The deeper teaching conveyed through this episode is that all Bhāgavatas who recite and celebrate the names of the Lord deserve reverence, irrespective of their age, social position, learning, or status. The greatness of a devotee is measured not by worldly qualifications but by devotion to Bhagavān and engagement in His remembrance.

Traditional history provides many examples illustrating this principle. One such incident concerns Mahāpūrṇar, the revered Ācārya of Rāmānuja. On one occasion, Mahāpūrṇar prostrated before a group of Śrīvaiṣṇavas who were returning from their ablutions in the Kāveri under the leadership of his own disciple, Rāmānuja. Although Rāmānuja was his disciple, Mahāpūrṇar saw in that assembly not merely individuals, but devotees of the Lord who were adorned with devotion and service. Therefore, he offered them his respects without hesitation.

In the same spirit, the heroine bows before the parrot. Her reverence is directed not towards the bird as an individual creature, but towards the sacred act of chanting the Lord's names. Through this beautiful episode, Āḻvār teaches that anyone who becomes a vehicle for the glorification of Bhagavān deserves honour and respect. The pāsuram thus highlights the exalted position of the Bhāgavata and the humility with which true devotees regard those who engage in the remembrance and praise of the Lord.
